3956.title: AI Sales Agent vs Chatbot vs Sales Rep: Which One Should a Distributor Use?
3956.text: .csku-sec{padding:24px 10px;color:#3b4252;font-size:16px;line-height:1.8}.csku-sec h2{color:#1a1a2e;font-size:30px;line-height:1.3;margin:0 0 16px}.csku-sec h3{color:#1a1a2e;font-size:19px;margin:22px 0 8px}.csku-sec p{color:#3b4252;margin:0 0 16px}.csku-sec a{color:#0d9488;text-decoration:underline}.csku-sec strong{color:#1a1a2e}.csku-sec figure{margin:18px 0 6px} Executive Summary A distributor deciding how to answer buyers faster has three real options: a rule-based chatbot, an AI sales agent, or more sales reps. They solve different problems. A basic chatbot answers a fixed list of questions and hands everything else to a person. An AI sales agent reads your catalog, understands a buyer's question in plain language, applies the right price, and turns the conversation into a request for quote. A sales rep does what neither can: negotiate, build trust, and close large accounts. For most distributors the best answer is not one or the other. Use an AI sales agent for the repeat product and quote questions that arrive at all hours, and keep your reps for pricing exceptions, relationships, and big deals. This post compares the three on the jobs that matter, shows the cost of each, and gives you a simple way to choose. Introduction Picture a distributor with 8,000 SKUs and a four-person inside sales team. By 10 a.m. the team has already answered the same questions: does this part come in stainless, what is the minimum order, can you quote 300 units by Friday. None of it is hard. All of it takes time, and the questions that arrive after 5 p.m. wait until the next morning. Three fixes usually come up. Add a chatbot. Add an AI sales agent. Or hire another rep. The names get mixed up because vendors call everything an "AI assistant", but the tools behave very differently once a real buyer asks a real question. If you are earlier in the process, our comparison of ChatGPT and a catalog chatbot covers why a general assistant is not the answer either. The short version: a chatbot follows a script, an AI sales agent follows your catalog and your rules, and a rep follows the relationship. The rest of this post shows where each one wins. What is the difference between an AI sales agent, a chatbot, and a sales rep? A traditional chatbot is a decision tree. It matches keywords to prepared answers, so it works for "What are your hours?" and breaks on "Do you have a 3/8 inch fitting in a 90 degree version?" When it cannot match, it says it did not understand, or it opens a form. An AI sales agent uses a language model connected to your product data. It reads the question the way a person would, looks up the product, applies the buyer's pricing, checks what it knows, and takes the next sales step, such as collecting quantity and ship-to details for a quote. It is built for selling, not only answering. A sales rep is a person. Reps are slow at repeat lookups and unavailable at night, but they read a room, negotiate terms, and spot an opportunity a system would miss. How do they compare side by side? Job to be done Rule-based chatbot AI sales agent Sales rep Answers a product question in plain language Only if the keyword matches Yes, from your catalog Yes, after looking it up Applies buyer-specific pricing No Yes, by customer group Yes Works at 9 p.m. and on weekends Yes Yes No Handles a typo or a vague question Rarely Yes Yes Builds a complete quote request Basic form only Yes, with quantity, ship-to, and contact Yes, manually Negotiates terms or custom pricing No No, routes to a rep Yes Builds trust on a large account No Limited Yes Cost to answer one more question Near zero Near zero Staff time When does a chatbot fall short for a B2B distributor? A scripted chatbot is fine for a store with 40 products and five common questions. A distributor is different. Catalogs are large, parts have close variants, and buyers ask about specs, substitutes, and quantities. Take a buyer who types, "Need a replacement for the old gasket on the 4 inch pump, probably the 2019 model." A keyword bot has nothing to match. The buyer leaves, or fills in a contact form and waits a day. That is the moment a chatbot loses the sale it was installed to protect. The other limit is the dead end. Many chatbots collect an email and stop. The team then has to go back, ask what the buyer wanted, and start over. The conversation had the information. The bot just could not use it. What does an AI sales agent do that a chatbot cannot? An AI sales agent is useful because it is connected to your data and to your sales process. In practice that means four things. First, it answers from your catalog, including spec sheets, PDFs, and ERP exports, so the answer matches what you sell. Second, it applies the right price for the buyer, so a wholesale account sees wholesale pricing. Third, it admits when it does not know and passes the buyer to a person instead of guessing. Fourth, it finishes the job: it gathers quantity, ship-to, and contact details and sends a complete request for quote to your team or your CRM. That fourth step is where most of the value sits. A good answer that ends in a closed chat window is a lost lead. A good answer that ends in a filled-in quote request is something your team can price first thing the next morning. We cover the full workflow in our guide to automating requests for quote . Where does a human sales rep still win? Reps win wherever the answer is not in a catalog. A buyer asking for a custom blend, a rebate tied to annual volume, or a new payment term needs someone who can make a decision. So does a buyer who has had a problem with a past order and wants to feel heard. Reps also win on large, slow deals. A first order of $60,000 usually comes after calls, samples, and a few emails from someone the buyer trusts. No software replaces that, and it should not try to. The useful way to think about it: reps are most valuable when they spend their day on decisions and relationships, not on looking up thread sizes. An AI sales agent takes the lookups off their plate so they have more time for the work only they can do. How much does each option cost a distributor? Compare the cost of answering a question, not the sticker price. A rule-based chatbot is often cheap, but it needs someone to write and maintain every answer, and it leaks leads when it cannot match a question. An AI sales agent is typically a fixed monthly plan, and the added cost of one more question is close to zero. A sales rep is the largest cost and the most valuable one. Salary, benefits, training, and software add up to a figure well beyond a software plan. Hiring a rep to answer repeat questions is like hiring an engineer to type up meeting notes: it works, but it uses an expensive person for work a system can do. A simple test: count how many of your team's weekly emails and chats are repeat product, stock, or quote questions. If it is more than a third, the first hire probably should not be a person. You can see current plans on the ChatSKU pricing page . How do you choose the right option for your business? Match the tool to the job. Use the questions below. If your catalog is small and your buyers ask five or six repeat questions, a rule-based chatbot may be enough. If your catalog is large, buyers use their own words, and you lose leads after hours, an AI sales agent fits. If your deals are few, large, and negotiated, invest in reps and use software only for the lookups. Most distributors land in the middle: a mixed model where the agent handles the first line and reps handle everything that needs judgment. Whatever you choose, test it on your own questions. Take ten real buyer messages from last week, including one with a typo, one after hours, and one asking for a part you do not sell. Score each answer as correct, wrong, or "did not know". Wrong answers matter more than missing ones. Our one-hour test gives you a ready checklist. What should you ask a vendor before you choose an AI sales agent? Whichever tool you shortlist, ask five plain questions. Where does the answer come from: your catalog, or the open internet? Does it apply each buyer's own price, or one list for everyone? What does it do when it does not know: guess, or hand over to a person? Can it send a complete quote request to your CRM or inbox, with quantity and ship-to attached? And who owns the conversation transcripts? The answers separate a script with a friendly face from a real sales tool. A vendor who is clear on all five has probably built for B2B. A vendor who changes the subject on pricing and "I don't know" has probably built for a store with forty products. Ask to see each one on your own parts, not on a prepared demo. Also ask how long it takes to go live and who maintains it afterwards. If setup needs a project team and a refresh calendar, the tool will drift out of date and your team will quietly stop trusting it. The best sign is a short setup and a catalog that updates when your files do. What does a mixed model look like in practice? A distributor with 8,000 SKUs adds an AI sales agent to the website. It answers product and stock questions around the clock, applies each buyer's pricing, and sends complete quote requests to the inside sales team. The team starts the day with a queue of ready-to-price requests instead of a pile of "can you call me?" emails. Reps then spend their time on the pricing exceptions the agent routes to them, the follow-ups on bigger quotes, and the calls that win large accounts. The agent never negotiates. It prepares. That split is the reason the model works: each one does the part it is best at. People Also Ask Is an AI sales agent the same as a chatbot? No. A chatbot follows a script. An AI sales agent understands the question, reads your catalog, applies the buyer's pricing, and moves the buyer toward a quote. Will an AI sales agent replace my sales team? No. It takes over repeat product and quote questions so your team has more time for negotiation, relationships, and large accounts. Can a chatbot give a customer a quote? A basic chatbot can collect an email. An AI sales agent can build a complete request for quote with quantity, ship-to, and contact details and send it to your team or CRM. How fast can a distributor set up an AI sales agent? With ChatSKU, setup is a single line of code on your site. See how it works on the AI sales assistant page . Conclusion Rule-based chatbots, AI sales agents, and sales reps are not rivals. A chatbot handles a short list of scripted questions. An AI sales agent handles the high volume of product, price, and quote questions in a distributor's day. A rep handles negotiation and trust. Put each on the job it does best. The fastest way to decide is to watch an agent answer your real products. You can request a demo built on your catalog . Frequently asked questions Does an AI sales agent work for small distributors? Yes. A smaller team often gains the most, because one person is usually answering the questions and building quotes at the same time. What happens when the agent does not know an answer? It says so and routes the buyer to your team, with the conversation attached, so the rep does not start from zero. What files can an AI sales agent read? Spec sheets, PDFs, Excel files, product feeds, and ERP exports are the common ones. Do buyers mind talking to an AI? Buyers mind slow answers more than the channel. Quick, correct replies with an easy path to a person are what they value. How do I measure whether it is working? Track quote requests captured, after-hours conversations, questions answered without a rep, and the questions the agent could not answer.

3929.title: Part number cross reference: the record nobody designed
3929.text: Executive Summary A part number cross reference is not a list of pairs. It is a record, and most distributors never designed it. Your table holds two numbers, but the buyer needs a decision. This article separates four relationships that people mix up: cross-reference, supersession, interchange, and substitute. Every row needs six fields: match type, what differs, direction, last verified date, stock, and next step. You also get a rule for who owns the table and what to say when nothing matches. Design the record first. Then decide who or what delivers it. Introduction Say a maintenance buyer is holding a worn part. The only clue is a number stamped by another maker. Her line is down, and she needs a replacement today. She types the number into your site. Nothing comes back, or a bare part number comes back with no context. Is the aftermarket equivalent you stock a drop-in replacement for that OEM part number? Is it only close? The page does not say. At your parts counter, a good rep asks which machine it is for and what has to match. Your table asks neither. Your cross-reference table stores two numbers in a row and nothing more. The buyer needs far more than that. This piece covers the record, its owner, and what to say on no match. A cross-reference table is a record nobody designed. It holds two numbers because that is all anyone needed when the first row was typed. What does a buyer holding another maker's number need? A buyer holding another maker's number needs a decision, not a lookup. Finding a matching number is only step one. The buyer still has to trust it enough to order. In practice, the buyer is doing four jobs at once. Each job needs a different part of the record. Find an equivalent. The buyer holds a competitor's number and wants your matching part. Check fit. Is the alternate part a drop-in or only a spec match, and what differs? Check supersession. The number may be obsolete, with a newer number in its place. Check stock and next step. Do you have it, and how does the buyer order? Most OEM cross reference lookup tools and equivalent part finders stop at the first job. That leaves fitment, supersession, and stock for the buyer to work out alone. How search reads your data is a separate topic, covered under retrieval mechanics . Where keyword search breaks is covered under keyword search failures . This article starts with the data. Is a cross-reference the same as a supersession? No, they are different relationships, and the difference decides what you tell the buyer. People use these words loosely. The table below shows how most parts counters use them, as general definitions and not an OEM standard. Term Whose number Direction What the buyer is told Cross-reference Another maker's number Either way, so state it This is an equivalent from a different maker Supersession Same maker, new number replaces old Often one way The old number was replaced by this one Interchange Either maker Usually two way These parts can be used in place of each other Substitute Your suggestion One way, from you This part is close, and here is what differs Pick one meaning for each word and use it everywhere. Mixed vocabulary is how a one-way supersession gets shown as an interchange. Why direction changes the answer Direction decides whether the old part still works. In a one-way supersession, the new part replaces the old one. The old one may not work where the new design is required. A two-way relationship means the parts are fully interchangeable. Now picture two buyers, as a hypothetical. The first holds the old number, so you can offer the new part. The second holds the new number and asks for the old one. Your answer may be no. If the old part is discontinued, say so. A buyer should never find that out after the order ships. Why one competitor number can map to several of your parts One-to-many is normal. One competitor number can point to several of your parts, each with a different finish, length, or rating. Each candidate needs its own list of differences. Show them as separate rows, not as one merged guess. The buyer then picks the functional equivalent that fits the job. What should one part number cross reference record hold? One record should hold six fields beyond the two numbers. They are match type, what differs, direction, last verified date, stock, and next step. The six fields Each field exists because a buyer asks the question it answers. Match type. Say if it is a direct replacement, a functional equivalent, or an application match. What differs. List the variance, such as thread, finish, or rating. Direction. State whether the match works one way or both ways. Last verified date. Show when a person last checked the row. Stock. Say whether you have the part now. Next step. Offer a quote, a hold, or a person. This is a way of describing matches, not an industry standard. Add the MPN and GTIN so the buyer can confirm the part. The numbers must also be readable text, which the catalog readability audit covers. What the buyer sees Here is a hypothetical example record. Every name and number in it is invented. Field What it says Buyer's number Maker A model 4410 Your part Your SKU 77-210 Match type Functional equivalent What differs Mounting holes are slightly wider, same rating Direction Two way Last verified A dated entry, with the name of who checked it Stock In stock at the main warehouse Next step Offer a quote, and a person confirms fit That record becomes a two-sentence answer for the buyer. "Your SKU 77-210 is a functional equivalent of Maker A model 4410, with wider mounting holes. It is in stock, and I can start a quote now." That answer is a candidate, not an approval. A person signs off on certified assemblies. Where the next step leads The next step often hits a limit. The buyer wants a few, and the part ships only by the case. Those minimum order rules belong in the record or in the next answer. Who keeps the table right? A named role must own the table, or it goes stale. Without an owner, every row ages at its own pace. Nobody knows which ones still hold. Where the table lives today Many ERP part records hold a linked number and a free-text note. Some have no field for match type or direction. So the rest lives in a rep's memory. That is a single point of failure. The rep retires, moves territories, or takes a week off, and the knowledge leaves too. What an owner actually does Name one role as owner, such as the product data lead. Stamp a date on every row. Review a row when a trigger fires. Triggers include a supplier change notice, a returned part, a buyer complaint, or a catalog update. Some manufacturers publish a disclaimer that specs between makers can differ. They add that they may not hear when an OEM changes one. If they cannot promise a match, a table nobody reviews cannot either. Export the table with its fields intact, and run an ERP export check before you upload it anywhere. ChatSKU answers from the table as you upload it. If the table is wrong, the answer is wrong. The data fix comes first. What should the answer say when there is no match? It should say there is no confirmed match, say what happens next, and never guess a close part. Say a buyer types a number at 8pm, and it is not in your table. A bad answer guesses a near-match and hopes. A good answer says there is no confirmed match and starts the next step. The bad answer sounds helpful, which is the danger. The buyer orders a guess, and your team inherits the return. What a good no-match answer contains A good answer does four things. It states the gap plainly. It asks for the specs or a photo. It captures contact details and quantity. It tells the buyer when a person will follow up. If you upload the table with the catalog, ChatSKU, an AI catalog assistant, answers from the rows it has. No row, no invented part. It then hands the buyer to a person or captures the quote request, at any hour. Files can be PDF, Excel, ERP exports, or CSV, as listed under supported catalog files . That is what AI product search should feel like: an answer from your data, or an honest no. How to hand the buyer to a person Route the buyer to a rep and pass everything along. Include the buyer's number, any specs, and the quantity so nobody asks twice. A handoff that repeats questions feels like a second dead end. If you are weighing who this suits, read about catalog assistant fit . People Also Ask What is a part number cross reference? A part number cross reference links one part number to another that does the same job. It usually maps another maker's number to yours, and it can run one way or both. A useful record also states the match type, what differs, and when someone last verified it. How do you find the equivalent of a competitor part number? Start with the cross-reference table from the maker or distributor you buy from. Search the competitor part number, then compare the listed differences against your need. If no row exists, send the number and specs to a person who can confirm a match before you order. Can a cross-reference be one-way? Yes, some relationships work in one direction only, such as a supersession. The new part may replace the old one, but the old part may not fit the new design. Make direction its own field, and check it before you order the reverse. Is an aftermarket equivalent the same as an OEM part? No, an aftermarket equivalent comes from a different maker and is built to do the same job. It may match the OEM part on fit and function, or differ in small ways. Check the listed variances, and get a person to sign off on certified assemblies. Conclusion Design the record first, then decide who or what delivers it. Every row needs six fields: match type, what differs, direction, last verified date, stock, and next step. Add an owner and a review trigger, and the table stops going stale. Add a clear no-match answer, and the buyer never meets a dead end. Start with the numbers buyers ask about most. See the ChatSKU live demo to watch an assistant answer from a table you upload. See the live demo Frequently asked questions Who should own the cross-reference table? Give it to one named role, usually product data or the parts desk lead. That person schedules reviews and approves changes. Reps can suggest edits, but one owner signs them off. How often should a row be re-verified? Re-verify on a trigger and on a calendar review. Triggers include a supplier change notice, a returned part, or a buyer complaint. Set the calendar cadence to match how fast your suppliers change parts. Can an assistant approve a substitute for a certified assembly? No, it can only present a candidate with the differences listed. A person signs off on certified assemblies. Treat every answer as a candidate, not an approval. What file format should I use to upload a cross-reference table? CSV or Excel works well, with one row per pair. That shape keeps each match type and difference on its own row. An AI catalog assistant reads PDF, Excel, ERP exports, and CSV, but tidy the table first. What if I have no cross-reference table yet? Start with the competitor part numbers buyers ask about most. Record those first, with every field above. Then grow the table from the questions your reps answer by hand.

3846.title: Your trade show booth closes at 5 pm. Your catalog can keep working.
3846.text: Executive summary Trade shows pack a year of buyer attention into two or three days. The serious conversations happen at the booth, but a large share of the real questions come later. A facilities manager walks the floor at 4 pm, wants to know whether a fitting comes in a 316 stainless version with a 50-piece minimum, and leaves with a business card. The rep sends a follow-up email the next morning. By then the buyer has already asked the same question at the booth next door. This guide explains where a catalog assistant fits into trade show follow-up. It covers which booth questions it can answer from your catalog files, which ones still need a person, how to prepare the catalog before the show, and what to do with the questions it cannot answer. It also covers how to tell whether the show produced more qualified conversations than a pile of business cards did. The plan works for a manufacturer or distributor with a catalog in PDF, Excel, or an ERP export, and a website that can carry one line of code. It does not require a developer on staff or a rebuilt site. Introduction: the question that arrives after the booth closes Consider an illustrative case: a mid-size industrial supplier at a regional maintenance show. The booth is busy from opening to close. Between conversations, the rep answers questions from memory, pulls a binder of spec sheets, and promises to send the rest. The catalog has several thousand SKUs spread across a PDF, two spreadsheets, and an ERP export that only the operations team reads. On the second afternoon, a buyer scans the QR code on the booth sign and types a question into the catalog page on the company website. It is 4:40 pm. The rep is packing up. The buyer wants stock availability for a specific size, a finish, and the price for an account that buys in volume. Without a catalog assistant, that question waits until morning. With one, the buyer gets an answer from the catalog files, or a clear note that a person will follow up, while the interest is still fresh. Many trade show teams have no way to answer a question at 4:40 pm on a Tuesday. The rest of this guide is about building one. Who uses a trade show catalog assistant? Three people touch the process, and each one needs something different from it. The booth rep needs fewer repeated questions during the show. The AI sales assistant for B2B ecommerce page describes the same question-answering flow from the buyer's side. A rep who spends the day answering "do you have this in stainless?" cannot hold a useful conversation with the buyer who needs a custom specification. The assistant takes the routine questions so the rep can spend the day on the conversations that need judgment. The sales manager needs a clean list of who asked what, and which questions went unanswered. Those unanswered questions are the most valuable output of the whole show, because they show where the catalog, the pricing rules, or the product range falls short of what buyers actually want. The owner or marketing lead needs to know whether the show was worth the cost. That answer depends on qualified conversations and their follow-up speed, not on how many people scanned the badge. Which booth questions can a catalog assistant answer on its own? The honest answer is that it depends on what is in your catalog files. A catalog assistant answers from the catalog it has been given, so the quality of the answer depends on the quality of the data. ChatSKU reads the files you already have, including PDF price lists, Excel sheets, ERP exports, and CSV files, and builds the assistant from them. Questions the catalog files can settle Some questions are factual and sit in the catalog. These include stock or availability for a listed item, the size, material, or finish options, the minimum order quantity, the case or pack size, and the lead time when it is written in the file. A buyer who asks these at 4:40 pm should get the answer immediately. Questions that still need a person Other questions depend on judgment or on information outside the catalog. Custom engineering, a special finish that is not in the file, a site visit, and negotiated contract pricing for a large account all belong to a person. A good assistant does not guess at these. It recognizes that the question is outside its catalog and passes it on with the buyer's details attached. Questions that depend on who is asking Pricing is the tricky category. If you sell with customer groups or tiered pricing, the price a buyer sees may depend on the account they belong to. Decide before the show which prices a visitor can see without signing in, which ones need an account, and which ones always come from a rep. Write those rules down, then check that the assistant follows them. A booth visitor who sees the wrong price has a worse experience than one who sees no price at all. How do you prepare the catalog before the show? Preparation matters more than the setup. The one-line script tag takes minutes to add to a page. Cleaning up the catalog takes weeks, and it is where most of the value comes from. Start with the SKUs that drive booth questions Look back at the last two shows, or at the last few months of inbound questions. Pick the products that buyers asked about most, and keep the list short enough that you can finish it before the show. Make sure those products have complete, consistent entries: size, material, finish, pack size, minimum order, and lead time. An assistant can only answer confidently about what it can read clearly. Reconcile the PDF with the spreadsheet Trade show catalogs are often built from a PDF that was last updated six months ago, while the spreadsheet has changed twice since then. Before the show, check the two against each other for the products you plan to feature. When they disagree, the assistant will reflect whichever file it reads, so pick the current one and retire the old one. The same check applies to ERP exports, which sometimes hold a unit of measure the printed catalog does not. Decide what the booth sign links to The QR code or short link on the booth sign should go to a page that already carries the assistant, not to a generic homepage. This is a small detail that changes how the show performs. The visitor lands on the page where the questions can be answered, and the rep does not have to explain the next step. For a sense of what a buyer does with this kind of tool before a purchase, the after-hours buyer problem covers the same behavior outside a trade show setting, and it is a useful companion when you decide which hours matter most. What should happen to a question the assistant cannot answer? This is where most trade show plans fall apart. The assistant answers the easy questions well. The hard ones either disappear or get routed to a shared inbox where they wait for two days. Turn each open question into a lead When the assistant cannot answer, it should capture the question, the product, the buyer's contact details, and the time. ChatSKU builds quote requests from the same catalog conversation, so a buyer who asks for a volume price can move into a request for quote without repeating what they already said. The request then goes into your existing workflow. Send the lead into the system your team already uses A lead from a trade show should land where the rest of your leads land. ChatSKU connects to CRM and ecommerce systems (see the feature overview ), so the captured questions can be sent into the tools your sales team already uses, instead of a separate spreadsheet that only one person checks. Confirm the specific connection with your implementation contact before the show, because the exact fields and the sync schedule depend on your setup. For a closer look at why speed matters once a quote is requested, the RFQ form best practices guide covers what a quote request needs to include, and the quote-to-order automation post explains what happens when the reply is slow. Set a response time before the show Decide how quickly each open question gets a human reply, for example by the next business morning, and assign one person to own that queue for the duration of the show. Without an owner, the captured questions are only a list. With one, they become the follow-up plan. How do you measure whether the show was worth it? Business card counts and scan totals tell you very little. A better measure is the number of conversations that reached a specific next step, such as a quote request, a sample request, or a scheduled call, and how long each one took to get a reply. Count qualified conversations, not contacts Separate the buyers who asked a specific question from the people who only picked up a brochure. Specific questions, such as a question about a finish or a volume price, are a stronger signal than a general interest in the company. Track those separately in the report you send after the show. Track the questions the catalog could not answer The unanswered questions are a free list of catalog gaps. If buyers keep asking for a size you do not list, or for a finish that exists only in a spec sheet, the catalog needs an update. Bring that list to the product team after the show. It will tell you more about what to add to the next catalog than any feedback form. Compare follow-up speed with last year If you attended the show before, compare the time between a question and a reply. A catalog assistant changes that number for the questions it can answer, and the queue process changes it for the rest. The difference is usually more useful than the total lead count. People also ask Does a trade show catalog assistant replace the booth rep? No. It answers routine, factual questions from the catalog, which frees the rep for conversations that need judgment, negotiation, or a relationship. The rep still closes the important deals. Do I need a tablet or a kiosk at the booth? Not necessarily. The buyer can use their own phone by scanning the code on the booth sign, which opens the catalog page on your website. A tablet at the booth is a useful extra for demonstrations, but it is not required for the assistant to work. Can I set this up in the weeks before a show? The technical setup is quick, but the catalog cleanup is not. The PDF catalog conversion guide covers how a static catalog turns into searchable data. Start the data work at least a few weeks before the show so the assistant reads current, consistent files. Leave time to test the questions buyers actually ask. What should I tell buyers who ask something after the show? Tell them when they will hear back and who will reply. A clear timeline is more useful than a fast reply to the wrong question, and it keeps the buyer from assuming the question was lost. Conclusion A trade show gives you two or three days of buyer attention, and the most specific questions often arrive after the booth closes. A catalog assistant answers the factual ones right away, captures the rest with the buyer's details, and passes them to the process your team already runs. The work that matters most happens before the show. Clean the files for the products buyers ask about, reconcile the PDF with the spreadsheet, and assign one person to own the open-question queue with an agreed reply time. Try it on your own catalog file to see which booth questions it can answer. See the live demo Frequently asked questions How quickly can a trade show page get a catalog assistant? The technical step is one line of code on the page the booth sign links to. The longer task is preparing the catalog files so the answers are accurate, which is worth doing before the show rather than during it. Which catalog formats can the assistant read? ChatSKU builds the assistant from catalog files in common formats, including PDF price lists, Excel spreadsheets, ERP exports, and CSV files. The cleaner and more consistent the file, the more reliable the answers. What happens to a question the assistant cannot answer? The assistant captures the question with the product, the buyer's contact details, and the time, then passes it on for a person to answer. Set a reply time and an owner before the show so the question does not wait in a shared inbox. Can the assistant show different prices to different buyers? It can, if your pricing uses customer groups or tiers. Decide which prices are visible without an account, which need one, and which always come from a rep. Test the rules before the show so the right price reaches the right buyer. Who should own the open-question queue during the show? One named person, ideally someone on the sales team. Agree on a reply time before the first day, such as the next business morning, so every captured question gets a human answer.

3798.title: Who a B2B catalog assistant is built for (and who should skip it)
3798.text: Executive Summary A B2B catalog assistant answers buyer questions from your own product catalog, at any hour. It helps most at manufacturers, distributors and wholesalers that sell to other businesses, hold a catalog with real complexity, and lose questions after the sales team leaves. It helps much less where the catalog is missing, where buyers never ask questions outside a contract portal, or where every order is custom engineered. This guide gives you a plain way to judge the fit. It covers the company profile that usually benefits, the people involved on both sides of the conversation, the features that matter for each kind of catalog, and the cases where you should wait or choose something else. You can run the whole test on your own files in about an hour. Introduction It is 7:40 on a weekday evening. A purchasing manager at a regional contractor has your catalog open in one browser tab and a spreadsheet in another. She needs to know whether a hydraulic fitting comes in a smaller pack, whether her account price applies at fifty units, and whether the lead time changes if she orders today. Your sales team went home at five. The catalog page shows the part but not the price she would see, and it does not answer the pack size question. She will not wait until morning for a callback. She will send the same three questions to two other suppliers before she closes her laptop. Most B2B companies have some version of this problem. The question this article answers is narrower: which companies have it badly enough, and in a way an AI catalog assistant can actually fix? Answering that honestly means looking at the company, the catalog, the buyers and the team that has to follow up. It also means being clear about when the answer is no. Which companies get the most from a catalog assistant? The best fit is a business that sells to other businesses and manages a catalog too large or too detailed for a static page. Manufacturers, distributors and wholesalers all match that pattern. Each one deals with product data that changes often, prices that vary by customer, and buyers who need an answer before they commit. Revenue and headcount give a rough guide, not a rule. Most companies that take this seriously sit somewhere between about $1 million and $50 million in annual revenue, with 10 to 200 employees. At that size you usually have real buyer volume and a catalog that one person can no longer answer alone, but you still feel every hire you would need to cover the gap. Company size matters less than three conditions. The catalog must be complex enough that buyers ask detailed questions. Buyers must ask those questions before they order. And someone must be able to act on the answers the assistant cannot give. If one of those is missing, the assistant has very little to do. What does a catalog assistant actually have to read? A catalog assistant is only as good as the data it can reach. Before you think about buyers, look at where your product information lives today. Most B2B companies keep it in one or more of these places: A PDF catalog that gets updated once or twice a year An Excel workbook or several spreadsheets, often with different column names An ERP export that holds stock, cost and price tiers A CSV file produced by a product information tool Each source has a different level of structure, and the assistant has to handle all of them. ChatSKU reads PDF, Excel, ERP and CSV sources, so you do not need to move everything into one clean database first. The practical check is simpler: can you export your product data in one of these formats today? If the answer is yes, you can start. If the only copy of your product knowledge is in a senior employee's memory, the catalog has to be written down before any assistant can use it. The PDF catalog guide explains why static PDFs cost sales even before any assistant is involved, and the PDF catalog chatbot page shows how a PDF-based catalog gets used. Data quality still counts. An assistant that reads an outdated spreadsheet will give confident wrong answers. Check how often your product data changes and who is responsible for updating it. A catalog that changes weekly needs a sync plan. A catalog that changes once a year can work with a periodic upload. Who are the buyers on the other side? The people typing into the assistant are usually purchasing managers, procurement leads, office managers at contractor firms, and buyers at resellers. They know their trade. They do not need a definition of a gasket or a pallet. What they want is specific: whether an item is in stock, what their price is at a given quantity, whether a substitute meets a spec, and how long a quote will take. Buyers arrive when it suits them, which is often outside your business hours. They also compare suppliers quickly. A buyer who gets a clear answer at 8pm is more likely to request a quote than one who waits two days for a reply. This is why the after-hours buyer problem matters more for some businesses than others. If your buyers mostly call during working hours and place orders with a rep, the assistant adds less. Buyers also judge the assistant by how it handles their own situation. If every buyer sees the same price, the assistant will fail the moment a long-standing account asks about its contract rate. That is why the way your company prices by customer group needs to be understood before you start, not after. What does the fit test look at? Before you buy any tool, answer five questions honestly. Each one points to a different part of the business. Does a usable catalog exist? Look at whether you can export product data in PDF, Excel, CSV or from an ERP today. If you cannot, the first job is cataloguing, not chat. Do buyers ask questions before they order? Check your last month of inbound email and phone notes. Count how many were about specs, stock, substitutes or price. If the answer is mostly "please send me the PO," the assistant has little to answer. Do different customers pay different prices? Customer groups and tiered pricing are a real complication for B2B. If every buyer sees one list price, the assistant's main advantage is smaller. If you run contract prices, volume breaks or distributor tiers, the assistant has to match each buyer to the right number. The tiered pricing guide covers why that matters online. Do questions arrive when your team is offline? Look at the timestamps on your inbound requests. A large share of requests after hours means a real gap. A small share means your team already covers the phone well. Is someone ready to act on a handoff? An assistant can capture a quote request or a question it cannot answer. Someone still has to respond. If that inbox is unowned, the assistant will only move the problem earlier in the process. Four or five yes answers suggest a strong fit. Two or three suggest a trial on one product line. Zero or one suggests waiting. The score is a guide for your own review, not a guarantee of results. Which catalog problems does an assistant solve, and which does it not? An assistant solves a specific problem: buyers who can find a product but cannot get an answer about it. Many companies have a passive catalog, which shows products clearly but cannot close a sale when a buyer has a question. The passive catalog problem describes this gap in more detail, and it is the clearest case for an assistant. An assistant does not solve a pricing agreement that has not been made, a warehouse that cannot ship, or a sales process that takes three weeks to reach a decision. It also does not fix an outdated catalog. The response gap, which is the delay between a buyer's question and a human reply, is a related problem. The response gap explainer explains how that delay usually builds up, and the response gap page covers the operating side of it. For a broader look at the category, the catalog chatbot guide explains what these tools do and what they do not do. Read it if you are still deciding whether the category itself makes sense for your business. Who should skip it? Some businesses should wait or choose a different approach. Better you hear it now than after a trial. You have no catalog file. If product knowledge lives only in people's heads or in paper binders nobody has digitized, there is nothing for the assistant to read. Build a structured catalog first. The catalog cost analysis can help you size the problem before you commit to a fix. Your buyers only order through a fixed contract portal. If every purchase runs through a customer's procurement system at pre-agreed terms, buyers rarely ask your website questions. The conversation happens somewhere else, and an assistant on your site will sit idle. Every product is custom engineered. If each order starts from a blank drawing and a long engineering discussion, there is no standard catalog to answer from. A quoting process built around engineers fits better here. Your catalog is very small. If a one-page price list answers almost every question, an assistant adds little. The value grows with catalog size and buyer volume. Nobody owns follow-up. If quote requests land in an inbox that nobody reads, the assistant cannot fix that. Solve the handoff process first, or the assistant will only capture requests that wait longer. What does setup involve in practice? Setup is simpler than most B2B software, but it is still work. The steps usually run in this order: Export your product data in the formats you already have. Review the data for obvious gaps, such as missing prices, duplicate SKUs or outdated pages. Add the one-line script tag to your site, which takes most teams under a day. Set up customer groups and tiered pricing so each buyer sees the right number. Connect the systems that matter, such as your CRM, ecommerce platform or ERP. Sync keeps the assistant current when stock or prices change. Test the assistant with real questions from your buyers, and check each answer against your own records. The test in step six takes the most time and matters most. Ask it the questions buyers actually send. Check every price and availability answer against your own system. Note the questions it cannot answer, because those show where your catalog or your follow-up process needs work. If your platform is WooCommerce or Magento, the integration details are different. The WooCommerce chatbot buyer's guide covers the questions to ask before choosing a tool for that platform. How do you know whether it is working? Measure the outcomes that matter to your business, not the number of chats. Useful measures include the share of buyer questions answered without a human, the number of quote requests that arrive after hours, how many of those requests become orders, and how long your team spends on repetitive catalog questions. Real-time analytics on buyer intent show what buyers ask about most, which products get questions without purchases, and where the catalog itself is unclear. Use that data to fix the catalog, not only to tune the assistant. A product that gets the same question every day probably needs a better specification, a clearer photo or a note on compatibility. For a rough financial check, the ROI calculator lets you model lost after-hours demand against your own order values. Treat the result as a starting estimate. Your real numbers will depend on conversion rates, order size and how fast your team follows up. What does this mean for your team? An assistant changes the work your team does. It does not remove the need for people. Reps spend less time on lookups and more time on deals that need judgment. Sales managers see which questions come up most. Ecommerce managers own the catalog data the assistant depends on. Owners see the cost of unanswered demand. Expect some internal change. Reps may worry about being replaced. Be clear that the assistant handles routine questions and prepares quotes, while people still negotiate and close. The question of whether AI will replace B2B sales reps covers that concern in more depth. Plan the handoff rules before launch so no quote request sits unclaimed. Also plan the minimum order rules. Buyers often hit a minimum at checkout, and an assistant that cannot explain the rule will frustrate them. The minimum order quantity guide covers how those rules create friction and how to answer them quickly. People Also Ask Is a B2B catalog assistant only for large companies? No. The better test is catalog complexity and buyer volume. A company with around ten people can benefit if it has thousands of SKUs, tiered pricing and buyers who ask detailed questions. A larger company with a short price list may gain less. Very small businesses may not have enough buyer questions to justify the setup. Does a catalog assistant replace a developer? Usually not for the basic setup. The most common method is a single script tag added to the site, which a team member who can edit the site header or a tag manager can add. Syncing with an ERP or CRM and setting up pricing rules can need more technical help, depending on how your systems are built. What should I do before I start a trial? Export your product data, list the twenty questions buyers ask most often, and decide who will handle quote requests. Those three items show quickly whether the assistant can work for you. They also give you a clear way to judge the trial result. Conclusion A B2B catalog assistant helps when buyers have detailed questions, your catalog is complex enough to be hard to answer by hand, and someone is ready to follow up. It helps less when the catalog is missing, the buyers order through a fixed portal, or every product is custom. The fit test in this guide is meant to show you which group your company falls into before you spend time on a trial. If the test points to a fit, the next step is a trial on one product line using your own catalog files and real buyer questions. Run the fit test on your own catalog before you decide. See the feature list Frequently asked questions What types of companies is a catalog assistant built for? Manufacturers, distributors and wholesalers that sell to other businesses. The usual profile has a real product catalog, buyers who need quotes, and a sales team that cannot answer every question during business hours. Who uses the assistant inside a company? Owners track the revenue effect. Sales managers use it to take repetitive spec and availability questions off their reps. Ecommerce managers handle the catalog data and the site setup. Buyers use it on the other side of the screen. What if my catalog is only PDFs or spreadsheets? That is enough to start. ChatSKU reads PDF, Excel, ERP and CSV sources, so you do not need a new database first. Check the data for gaps before you go live, because the assistant can only answer from what it reads. Does it work if buyers pay different prices? Yes, if your pricing is set up in the system. Customer groups and tiered pricing are built in, so each buyer sees the price that matches their account. Confirm the rules with a test account before you rely on them. Can I use it if my buyers order through a contract portal? Probably not for ordering. If purchases run only through a fixed procurement portal, buyers rarely ask questions on your website. The assistant adds the most value where buyers browse, ask questions and request quotes. How long does setup take? The script tag can go live in under a day. Reviewing the catalog, setting up pricing rules and testing real buyer questions takes longer, and the testing step matters most.

3767.title: Where should a BigCommerce B2B quote request start?
3767.text: Executive summary A BigCommerce B2B quote request should start where it can end as a complete, correctly priced request a rep can act on. Test every path against four checks: a complete request, the right price for this company, an answer after hours, and a rep-ready handoff. A quote form suits custom work where the buyer knows the part. Live chat suits a store with a person online and a nuanced question. An AI catalog assistant suits complete, correctly priced requests at any hour, with reps still approving. Most stores end up combining them. Introduction It's 8pm, and a buyer wants a mixed order from your BigCommerce store. The best place for that quote request to start is wherever it can end as a complete, correctly priced request. For most stores with company price lists, that means a chatbot built as an AI catalog assistant, working next to a form for custom jobs. Buyers are leading these conversations now. 6sense's 2025 buyer report found that buyers start about 79% of first contacts themselves. The same report found that buyers spoke to the eventual winner first 77% of the time. That doesn't prove the fastest reply wins. It does mean the entry point is where the first conversation happens . Here is how to decide. What does a good first quote conversation have to do? It has to pass four checks. Each one is a job a rep would otherwise do by hand the next morning. Complete request. Items, quantities, pack sizes, and ship-to are all there. Right price for this company. The price matches the buyer's account, not the public list. Answered after hours. The buyer gets a real response while your team is offline. Rep-ready handoff. The rep opens something to approve, not something to decode. No path scores perfectly on all four. The next three sections score each one honestly. Where does a quote form hold up, and where does it break? A form holds up for custom work where the buyer knows exactly what they need. It breaks when the request needs checking, because a form can't check anything. A form captures fields and waits. It queues until a rep opens it, so an 8pm request sits until morning. That wait is the classic after-hours buyer problem , and a form alone doesn't solve it. Price is the bigger gap. A form can't tell whether the quantity makes sense or the price is right for this company. Native quoting sits in B2B Edition, which you enable on the store, and many stores use an app-based form instead. BigCommerce's documentation for creating quotes treats a quote with no company or customer ID as a guest quote. A guest has no company price list, so a rep reprices it by hand. Scored against the four checks, a form captures only what the buyer typed. It doesn't verify the price, it receives without answering, and it hands over raw fields. When is live chat the right front door? Live chat is the right front door when a person is reliably online and the question is a nuanced one. A good rep can read the situation, ask the sharp follow-up, and close a tricky job. The limits are mechanical. Chat covers staffed hours only. The rep still looks up the company's price, and a transcript is not a structured quote. Someone has to turn the conversation into line items. Scored against the four checks, chat completes a request only as well as the rep's questions do. The price depends on a lookup, and after hours the widget is offline. The handoff is a transcript. If your team sits online during the hours buyers ask, and most requests are custom, chat may be all you need. That is a legitimate answer. Before you commit, check what your catalog data can support, starting with what ChatSKU connects to . What does an AI catalog assistant need before it can quote? It needs your catalog and the buyer's own pricing. Without them it quotes list price, which is worse than having no assistant at all. BigCommerce prices can differ by company, and price lists attach to customer groups. So the assistant has to read company accounts, price lists, and customer groups. If the price list is wrong in BigCommerce, the quote will be wrong too. With that data, the work is specific. It asks the missing questions, such as size, quantity, and ship-to. It applies the customer group price, drafts the quote, and hands the rep a complete package. The rep still decides. The BigCommerce B2B Edition introduction notes that reps can review and edit quoted prices, which is why the assistant hands off rather than approves. One line of code installs ChatSKU for BigCommerce , and stores go live in under a day with no rebuild. Buyers are ready for this. McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey, as reported by Digital Commerce 360 , found that 39% of buyers would spend over $500,000 per order. Those orders went through self-serve or remote channels. Large orders already happen without a rep call What does one 8pm mixed order look like under each path? The same order lands very differently on each path. Only one puts a complete draft in front of the rep at 9am. Illustrative example. A distributor sells on BigCommerce with company accounts and a negotiated price list. At 8pm on a weeknight, a buyer for an established customer wants a mixed order. It has several SKUs in different pack sizes, plus one item the buyer isn't sure you carry. Quote form. The buyer fills in what they know and leaves the uncertain item as a free-text note. The rep opens it the next morning and finds a missing quantity. The price needs checking against the company's list, so the rep writes back. The first real conversation starts at 9am. Live chat. The widget shows offline. The buyer emails or leaves. AI catalog assistant. The buyer types the order in plain words. The assistant matches the SKUs and asks for the one missing quantity. It applies the company's price list and flags the uncertain item for a rep. The morning queue holds a complete, priced draft and one flagged question. The difference is not speed alone. It is what the rep opens first. Everything here ends when the request reaches the rep, and what follows is a separate problem, the silence after the quote . How do you choose between the three paths? Ask three questions in order. The first one you answer yes to tells you where to start. A side-by-side table follows the People also ask section. Do most requests need custom engineering or a one-off price? Then use a form plus a rep. Is a person reliably available during the hours buyers ask? Then add live chat. Do buyers have company price lists and send mixed or large catalog orders after hours? Then an AI catalog assistant earns the front door. The paths combine. The form doesn't disappear, because custom jobs still need one. If your goal is quoting in under an hour , a request that arrives complete does most of the work. A few practical lessons hold on any path: Model the numbers first with the ROI calculator . Decide what a "complete" request means before you automate anything. Keep approval with a human. Test prices against a real company account before launch. Keep the form for the jobs that need one. People also ask Is a quote form or live chat better for B2B quote requests? Neither wins on its own. A form suits custom work where the buyer knows the need, and chat suits moments when a person is online. Both leave gaps on price correctness and after-hours coverage. Can a chatbot build a B2B quote with the customer's own pricing? Yes, but only if it reads that customer's price list or customer group. Without live price data it quotes list price. The same assistant should assemble the items, quantities, and handoff, not just a number. What happens to a quote request that arrives after hours? With a form, it queues until a rep opens it. With live chat, it usually goes unanswered. An AI catalog assistant can finish the request on the spot and leave a complete package for morning. Can a chatbot show the right price for each customer group? Yes, if it is connected to the customer group and price list data on the store. It should show the group's price to a recognised buyer and flag anything it can't confirm. Quote form vs live chat vs AI catalog assistant: side by side Here is the whole comparison for BigCommerce quote workflows in one place. Read across a row to see how each path handles one check. Check Quote form Live chat (human) AI catalog assistant Complete request Only what the buyer typed Depends on the rep's questions Asks for missing size, quantity, and ship-to Right price for this company Not checked, the rep reprices The rep looks it up Applies the price list or customer group, flags exceptions Answered after hours Partly: received, not answered No: offline Yes: answered at any hour Rep-ready handoff Raw fields A transcript A structured, priced draft with the conversation attached Setup Low: an app or theme change Low, but needs staffing One line of code, live in under a day What the buyer sees at 8pm A confirmation and a wait An offline widget A conversation that finishes the request What the rep receives A queue of uneven requests Whatever was said in the chat A complete draft quote to approve or adjust One honest limit sits under the table. The assistant is only as good as the catalog and price data it reads. Conclusion The question was never form or chat. It is where the first quote conversation happens, and whether it ends in something a rep can act on. Use a form for known-part custom work. Use live chat when someone is really there. Give the rest, the mixed orders and the 8pm requests, to an AI catalog assistant. It reads your buyer’s own prices, and your team keeps the approval. See it handle a quote request on your own catalog. See the live demo Frequently asked questions How quickly can we get quote requests running on BigCommerce? ChatSKU goes on your current site as a single line of code. Most stores go live within a day, since it reads your current catalog files instead of waiting on a rebuild. Do we need to replace our quote form or rebuild our catalog first? No. Keep the form for known-part custom work. Your current catalog files are enough, whether that is a spec sheet, a spreadsheet export, or an ERP file, so there is no migration step. Does it quote with each customer group’s own pricing? Yes. It applies each buyer’s customer group and tiered pricing to the answer. A contract account and a first-time buyer do not see the same price for the same part. Does this replace our sales reps? No. It collects and prices the request, then hands your team a structured quote. Reps approve it, handle custom engineering, and own the relationship. What if our catalog data is messy or incomplete? It works from the files you already have. Gaps show up as questions it cannot answer yet, which tells you exactly what to clean up first.

3848.title: ChatGPT vs a Catalog Chatbot for B2B Product Questions
3848.text: ﻿ .csk-card{background:#f9f9fb;color:#374151;padding:40px 44px;border-radius:6px;margin:0 0 40px}.csk-card h2,.csk-card h3{color:#1a1a2e}.csk-card p,.csk-card li,.csk-card td,.csk-card th,.csk-card summary{color:#374151}.csk-card a{color:#0f9d8a;text-decoration:underline}.csk-card .csk-faq summary{color:#1a1a2e}@media(max-width:600px){.csk-card{padding:24px 18px}} .csk-note{background:#f1f5f9;border-left:4px solid #2dd4bf;padding:16px 20px;margin:20px 0}.csk-tablewrap{overflow-x:auto;margin:20px 0}.csk-cmp{width:100%;border-collapse:collapse;font-size:15px;line-height:1.5}.csk-cmp th{background:#0f172a;color:#fff;text-align:left;padding:12px 14px;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif;font-weight:600}.csk-cmp td{padding:12px 14px;border-bottom:1px solid #d5d8dc;vertical-align:top;color:#1a1a2e}.csk-cmp td:first-child{font-weight:600}.csk-faq{border:1px solid #d5d8dc;border-top:none;background:#fff}.csk-faq:first-of-type{border-top:1px solid #d5d8dc}.csk-faq summary{list-style:none;cursor:pointer;padding:15px 20px;color:#1a1a2e !important;font-family:'Space Grotesk',sans-serif;font-size:16px;font-weight:600}.csk-faq summary::-webkit-details-marker{display:none}.csk-faq summary::before{content:"+";display:inline-block;width:24px}.csk-faq[open] summary{color:#e0505f !important;border-bottom:1px solid #d5d8dc}.csk-faq[open] summary::before{content:"−"}.csk-faq p{padding:15px 20px;margin:0} Executive summary Many B2B owners already pay for ChatGPT and ask the obvious question: can we use it for our catalog and let it answer buyers? For internal work such as drafting replies and summarizing spec sheets, it helps. For answering a buyer's product question on your website, it runs into five problems. It does not know the price this buyer should pay. It does not see current stock or lead times unless someone keeps feeding it. It can state a spec with confidence when your source says something else. It cannot turn a question into a quote. And the conversation leaves your control. A catalog chatbot is built around those five problems. This post compares the two on the questions B2B buyers actually ask, says where ChatGPT is the right tool, and gives you a one-hour test to run on your own catalog before you decide. Introduction Picture a distributor with 12,000 SKUs, three price lists, and a sales team that spends the morning answering the same thread-size and substitute-part questions. Someone in marketing says what many people say: we already have ChatGPT, so why not upload the price list and let it answer? It is a fair question, and it is getting more common because buyers are doing the same thing from their side. More of the first research on suppliers is now done by software, a shift we cover in what agentic commerce means for B2B owners . If software is asking about your products, the answer it finds has to be correct, current, and tied to the right customer. That is the standard to hold ChatGPT and any catalog chatbot to. The short version: ChatGPT is a very good writer and reader. A catalog chatbot is a very good lookup, built on top of a model like ChatGPT. The difference is not how well they talk. It is what they are connected to and who answers when they are wrong. The rest of this post walks through where that difference shows up, using the questions your buyers send every day. Can ChatGPT answer questions about a B2B catalog? Yes, within limits. Give it a spec sheet and it will summarize it, compare two products, and draft a clear reply. That works well for one rep, one document, and one afternoon, because the rep reads the answer before it goes anywhere. The job changes when the question comes from a stranger on your website at 9 p.m., about any of your 12,000 products, and nobody reviews the answer. At that point the work is no longer language. It is retrieval, pricing rules, and accountability for what was said. A simple example. A buyer asks, "Does the 3/8 inch stainless fitting come in a 90 degree version, and do you have 200 in stock?" That is three separate lookups: the product family, the variant, and live inventory. A general assistant can only answer the first one from whatever you pasted in. The other two need a connection to your data, and ChatGPT on its own does not have one. Does ChatGPT know the price this buyer should pay? No. B2B pricing is rarely one number. It depends on the customer group, the contract, the quantity break, and sometimes the ship-to location. A distributor may sell the same part at $4.10 to a walk-in buyer and $3.42 to a wholesale account on a volume tier. If you paste a price list into ChatGPT, it can only quote what is in that list, and it has no idea which buyer is asking. If the list contains negotiated prices, you have also copied commercial terms into a tool outside your systems. A catalog chatbot applies the price rules for the logged-in buyer, so the wholesale account sees the wholesale price and a new visitor sees the public one. What happens to the answers when your catalog changes? With ChatGPT, you re-upload. Every new product, discontinued part, and price change needs someone to refresh the file, and nobody is assigned to notice when the file goes stale. The failure is quiet: the answer still sounds right, it is just last quarter's answer. A catalog chatbot reads from the files and systems you already maintain, such as your product feed, spec sheets, and ERP exports, and refreshes when they change. The rule of thumb: if a human has to remember to update it, it will be out of date within a month. Will it make up an answer when it does not know? It can. General assistants are tuned to be helpful, which means they tend to produce a fluent answer even when the source is silent. In a casual chat that is a small annoyance. In B2B it can mean a wrong thread type, a wrong voltage, or a compatibility claim your team now has to honor or walk back. Here is a real pattern we see in testing. Ask any assistant for a part that is not in your catalog, such as a competitor's model number. A general model often suggests a "close equivalent" with a confident specification. A catalog chatbot is designed to say it does not have that product and hand the buyer to a rep. That one behavior, saying "I don't know" at the right time, is worth more to a B2B team than a smoother tone. Can it turn a question into a quote? A buyer rarely wants an answer for its own sake. They want a quote or an order. ChatGPT ends at the answer. A catalog chatbot continues: it collects quantity, ship-to, and contact details, and passes a complete request for quote to your team or your CRM, including outside business hours. This is where the revenue difference sits. A good answer that ends in a closed chat window is a lead lost. A good answer that ends in a filled-in request for quote is a lead your team can price on Monday morning. Our AI chatbot buyer's guide covers what to look for in that handoff. Where does the conversation go? When a buyer asks a public assistant about your product, you never see the question. Even on your own site, you need clear answers on who stores the transcripts, who owns them, and how they are used. An on-site catalog chatbot gives you the questions buyers asked, including the ones you could not answer, which is useful product and content data in its own right. Think of it as a free market research feed. The unanswered questions tell you which specs are missing from your product pages, which substitutes buyers look for, and which terms they use that your catalog does not. What about custom GPTs and file uploads? A custom GPT is the best version of the ChatGPT approach, and it is worth trying as a prototype. You can load your spec sheets, give it instructions, and share it with your team. Many companies get real value from this internally. The gaps appear when you try to put it in front of buyers. It does not log buyers in, so it cannot apply their pricing. It does not connect to live inventory. It does not hand a qualified lead to your CRM. And you would still own the upkeep of every file. If you are curious how far a prototype can go, run the test later in this post and see which questions it misses. How do ChatGPT and a catalog chatbot compare side by side? A catalog chatbot is built around those five problems. General assistants are tuned to be helpful, which means they tend to produce a fluent answer even when the source is silent. In a casual chat that is a small annoyance. They want a quote or an order. ChatGPT ends at the answer. An on-site catalog chatbot gives you the questions buyers asked, including the ones you could not answer, which is useful product and content data in its own right. Think of it as a free market research feed. You can load your spec sheets, give it instructions, and share it with your team. Many companies get real value from this internally. The gaps appear when you try to put it in front of buyers. It does not log buyers in, so it cannot apply their pricing. It does not connect to live inventory. It does not hand a qualified lead to your CRM. And you would still own the upkeep of every file.
