Their price depends on class, size, delivery address, and the seller's own carrier rate. None of that lives on a typical product page. What is the difference between LTL freight and parcel shipping? Parcel shipping covers small boxes at flat published rates, usually under about 150 pounds. LTL means less-than-truckload freight. It covers pallets that share truck space with other companies' goods. LTL is priced by class and size, not a flat rate. Why do two B2B buyers get different shipping quotes for the same product? Carriers set rates per shipper account, not per product. The cost to ship the same pallet can vary by account. It also varies by which carrier the seller uses. What information does a supplier need before they can quote freight shipping? A supplier needs the item's weight, size, and freight class. They also need the delivery address. Only then can they price extras like liftgate or residential delivery. Without all of that, any number is a guess. Conclusion The shipping-cost question is hard for a simple reason. The honest number depends on facts you don't have until the buyer shows up. Freight class, size, delivery address, and your own rate all have to line up first. None of that makes the question impossible to answer. The right catalog and quote workflows can route that moment faster. The buyer isn't left waiting on an inbox. Get the data right, and the silence gets a lot shorter. See the live demo Frequently asked questions What is LTL freight? Less-than-truckload freight, where a shipment shares truck space with other companies' freight. It's typically used for palletized shipments over roughly 150 pounds. What is a freight class? A freight class is a category from 50 to 500, set by the National Motor Freight Classification system. It's based on density, stowability, handling difficulty, and liability risk, and it's a main input into LTL cost. What is dimensional weight in shipping? Dimensional weight prices a shipment by the space it occupies: length times width times height, divided by a standard factor. Carriers bill whichever is higher, actual or dimensional weight. What are accessorial charges in freight shipping? Accessorial charges are extra fees for services beyond standard dock-to-dock delivery. Liftgate service, residential delivery, and inside delivery are common examples. Why do freight quotes change even for the same route? Fuel surcharges are calculated as a percentage of the base rate, tied to a fuel-price index. They adjust on a schedule, often weekly, so the same route can price differently week to week. Can B2B ecommerce sites show real-time freight rates? Yes, but only with clean data. The catalog needs weight, size, and freight class per SKU. The store also needs a live carrier account link. Without that, a rate widget shows the wrong number.

3010.title: Will AI replace your B2B sales reps? What actually changes for your team
3010.text: Executive summary AI doesn't take your rep's job away. It takes over the repeat lookups, spec questions, and price checks that eat most of their day. This article walks through what changes for four people: the rep, the sales manager, a brand new hire, and the owner. Each one sees the job shift, not disappear. We're just as honest about what breaks. A careless rollout can waste the whole opportunity, and this piece covers exactly how that happens. Introduction It's 9am on a Tuesday. Your rep opens their inbox to four emails. Two buyers want the same spec sheet you sent out yesterday. One needs a stock check before placing an order. A repeat customer wants "the same as last time, but in stainless." None of that is selling. It's lookup work, and it happens before your rep gets to a single real call. That's the actual job today, before anything changes. The real question isn't "will this replace me." It's "what does my week look like without the repeat stuff in it." How does a rep's day change? The repeat work moves to the assistant. The judgment calls stay with your rep. Spec questions, stock checks, and "what's my price on this" all get answered right away, day or night. Your rep never touches most of them. What stays with them is everything the assistant can't do well: negotiating a tough deal, handling an exception, reading a buyer about to walk. Those calls need a person who knows the account. Sales reps spend just 28% of their week on real selling, per Salesforce's 2023 State of Sales research. The other 72% goes to admin, data entry, and deal management, per that same Salesforce study. That leftover time is exactly where a catalog assistant does its work. Not on the call where your rep closes the deal. On the four emails that came in before it. Curious what's actually happening behind the screen? See how a catalog assistant answers , in plain terms. How does the sales manager's week change? You get fewer status-chase pings and a lot more visibility into what your buyers are actually asking. Instead of chasing your team for updates, you can just look. Spec requests, stock checks, and pricing questions all land in one place. That's a real shift in how you spend a Monday morning. Here's the part that matters most. What you do with the extra hours matters more than getting them in the first place. A manager who doesn't change what they measure won't see much benefit from any of this. More on that shortly. The assistant also speeds up what happens right after a quote request lands. See how quote to order automation closes that gap once pricing is settled. What's different for a brand new hire? A new rep still needs months to build real judgment about accounts and deals. What changes is how they spend that time. Instead of hunting through folders or asking a coworker where a spec sheet lives, a new hire gets the answer right away. That frees up their first few weeks for learning the accounts, not the paperwork. How long is "months," exactly? Ramp time for new B2B sales hires runs from around three months up to nearly six, per Bridge Group research. That data comes from software sales teams, not distributors, so treat it as a rough guide, not an exact number for your shop. There's a real risk worth naming here too. A brand new rep can lean on the assistant instead of learning the catalog. That's worth watching for in someone's first month on the job. What does the owner see change? You get to see the questions your reps used to handle quietly, on their own. Every spec check and price question used to disappear into someone's inbox. Now it shows up as data you can actually look at. That's real pipeline visibility, not a guess based on gut feel. It also means fewer leads slipping through the cracks after hours, when nobody's at a desk to answer. If you run a manufacturing or distribution business, this is exactly where an AI sales assistant earns its keep. It's built for distributors and wholesalers , not generic retail. Want to know what that's worth in your own numbers? The math is worth running, but we won't hand you a made-up percentage here. Is AI actually cutting sales jobs anywhere? In a few corners, yes. For most small sales teams, no. Here's the honest picture. Forrester expects about 6% of US jobs to be automated by 2030. That same Forrester forecast puts roughly 20% in the augmented column instead. Forrester also found that more than half of AI-blamed layoffs get quietly reversed once companies feel the real cost of losing people too fast. Where cuts are real, they land hardest on the most repetitive roles. Emergence Capital's April 2025 research found software companies cut entry-level sales roles at 36%, mid-level roles at 25%, and specialist roles at just 14%. Here's the catch, in the same breath. That's software industry data from venture-backed companies, not distributors. It doesn't map cleanly onto your two or three person inside sales team. Even the sources predicting job loss agree on what stays human. That's relationship-building on bigger accounts, working through multiple stakeholders, and judgment calls that don't fit a pattern. Curious how far this actually goes? Here's what agentic commerce means for a catalog, in plain English. What goes wrong when the rollout is careless? Plenty, and it's worth naming plainly. There's no single study to point to here. This is what people in the trade consistently see when a rollout goes sideways. Reps quietly work around a tool they don't trust. That trust breaks the first time the assistant gives a wrong stock number or an old price. It's slow to earn back. Check its answers yourself for a week before buyers ever see it. Start with one product line, not the whole catalog. Nobody owns the handoff. A lead the assistant captures goes cold if nobody owns picking it up. That's exactly like a shared inbox nobody checks. Here's what happens when the response gap opens up after the first reply, not just before it. Name one person who owns every lead it captures. Put it in writing. The manager doesn't change what they measure. If "calls made" stays the scoreboard after routine questions move to the assistant, the freed-up hours get eaten by busywork instead of real selling. Change the scoreboard on day one. Count quotes sent and deals won, not calls made. A new rep leans on the assistant instead of learning the catalog. That's the same crutch risk we flagged earlier, and it's worth watching in someone's first few months. Have them sit with a senior rep on the harder calls anyway. None of these four are technology problems. Each one is a decision somebody forgot to make. People also ask Does AI eliminate the need for a sales team? No. It takes over the repeat lookups and admin that eat most of a rep's week. That frees your team to spend more time on the calls that actually close deals. What can't AI do in B2B sales? Negotiation, handling exceptions, working multi-stakeholder deals, and judgment calls that don't fit a pattern. Those all still need a person who knows the account. Will a catalog assistant make my newest rep worse at their job? Only if nobody watches for the crutch risk. A new hire who leans on the assistant instead of learning the catalog can fall behind on judgment. Worth checking on in month one. Conclusion The tool changes what fills your rep's day. It doesn't change whether your team exists. Your reps stop drowning in spec sheets and stock checks. They spend more time on the calls that actually close deals. What happens in the first 90 days after rollout decides whether that turns into a stronger team or a stalled one. That part is on the manager, not the software. See the live demo Frequently asked questions How long does it take to roll out an AI catalog assistant for a small sales team? Most small teams are live within days, not months. It reads the product files you already keep, so nothing has to be rebuilt. Will it work with the way we already price customer groups and tiers? Yes. Tier and contract pricing are handled, so each buyer is quoted their own agreed rate. What happens to a lead it captures after hours? It gets routed to your team the next morning, or sooner if you set it up that way. Someone still needs to own the follow-up. Do we need to change our CRM or website to use it? No. It connects to your existing site with one line of code, and it can sync with the CRM you already run. Does this replace an experienced rep who already knows every account? No. Relationship-building on complex accounts stays with your best people. That's the part no assistant can replicate. What does the assistant need from our catalog to get started? Whatever you already have. PDFs, spreadsheets, or an export from your ERP are enough to get started, no clean-data project required first. Check the catalog integration options for the full list of formats.

2974.title: 9 Eras deep dive: what Era 07 (AI-enabled ChatCommerce) looks like in practice
2974.text: Executive summary You probably think your catalog has reached Era 07. The 9 Eras tool disagrees, and it isn't being coy about it. Era 07, AI-enabled ChatCommerce (2025-2028), is the era where the catalog itself answers in its own words, down to the spec, with tier-aware pricing surfaced mid-conversation instead of a static price sheet. Most sellers who bought some flavor of AI chat in the last two years assume that box is checked. To see how we got here, read the full evolution of B2B ecommerce . The tool scores Era 07 only partly machine-readable, not fully, and that one word carries the whole argument. Answering a person in seconds and exposing a catalog so another piece of software can query it are two different jobs. Era 07 solves the first. Era 08 needs both. The fix isn't a bigger chat widget. It's structured price and spec data a system can read without a human-phrased conversation sitting in the middle. That's what this piece walks through, using the tool's own five measures as the scorecard. Introduction It's 9:14pm on a Tuesday. A maintenance manager three states away needs a replacement part before a line goes down at 6am. He isn't browsing. He wants one answer: does this fit, and what does it cost at his volume. Your chat window pops open. It answers in two seconds. Somewhere in a meeting last quarter, someone said "we're covered, we bought the AI chat," and everyone nodded and moved to the next agenda item. Score your own catalog against the 9 Eras tool before you finish reading this. Its five measures make a case that a fast answer and a right answer are not the same claim, and most sellers are conflating them right now. Era 07 sits in the middle of the framework, past basic online buying, short of a catalog other software can query on its own. If you think you've already arrived, there's a good chance you're standing exactly here, one step short of where you assumed. What is Era 07 (AI-enabled ChatCommerce), and why do most sellers think they're already there? Era 07 (2025-2028) is the era where a catalog answers a buyer in natural language, down to the spec, in seconds, with tier-aware pricing shown as part of the conversation rather than looked up separately. That's the tool's definition, and it's a narrower claim than "we have AI chat now." The false positive is easy to explain. Most "AI chat" purchased between 2024 and 2025 was trained on policies, hours, and shipping information, not on the catalog itself. That's a real, useful thing to have. It just isn't Era 07. The tool's own predecessor is worth a look if you want the informal, earlier version of this thinking: the B2B commerce evolution sketched a rougher version of this progression before the current framework scored each stage on five specific measures. This piece stays inside those five measures rather than reopening that older model. The distinction matters most for distributors and wholesalers running catalogs with real complexity: thousands of SKUs, customer-specific pricing, and specs that decide whether a part actually works, not just whether it's in stock. A generic policy bot has nothing to say about any of that. A catalog-grounded assistant does. Why does an Era 06 chat widget feel like Era 07, but fail on the question that matters? Because Era 06 is trained on policies, hours, and shipping, not on the catalog itself, so it hands off the conversation exactly when a buyer gets specific. It feels like Era 07 for the first ten seconds. Then someone asks a real question. Here's a test you can run today, on your own site, in under a minute. Open your existing chat widget and ask it something like: "Do you have a 30-amp, 480-volt connector in stock, and what's the price at 500 units?" Use a real part from your own catalog if you have one handy. If the widget answers with a SKU, a spec confirmation, and a tier price, you're closer to Era 07 than most of your competitors. If it asks for your email address or offers to connect you with a representative tomorrow, you're at Era 06, no matter what the vendor called it when you bought it. Measure Era 05 Era 06 Era 07 Time to an answer Immediate, if the SKU is already known Instant, then a handoff Seconds Who does the answering Filters and a search box A script, then a person tomorrow The catalog itself Price visibility Tiered and visible Out of scope for the bot Tier-aware, mid-conversation At 9pm on a Tuesday Checkout works fine It replies. It does not answer No difference from 9am Machine-readability Not machine-readable Not machine-readable Partly machine-readable Read down that last row and the whole article is right there. Getting from Era 05 or 06 to Era 07 is a real jump. Getting the last column to say "yes" instead of "partly" is a different jump entirely, and it's the one most sellers haven't started. For the fuller definition of this category and the ROI math behind it, B2B conversational commerce covers that ground. This section's only job is diagnosing which era your current widget actually sits in. What can a fully built B2B eCommerce platform still not answer? A modern storefront with search and filters, Era 05 in the tool's framework, handles checkout and known-SKU lookups just fine. What it can't do is judge whether a part actually fits the application a buyer is describing, because its search returns matches for the words someone typed, not a decision about suitability. This is worth sitting with, because it's where most well-funded sellers actually live. You replatformed. You have filters, faceted search, saved carts, maybe a customer portal with negotiated pricing built in. By any reasonable standard, you're modern. And you can still fail the 9pm test. A buyer who already knows their SKU checks out fine at 2am. A buyer who describes a problem instead of a part number gets a results page, not an answer. Most readers who tell themselves "we're past that stage" mean they're solidly at Era 05. That's a real accomplishment. It isn't Era 07. Why does the tool score Era 07 only "partly" machine-readable? Because answering a human in natural language and exposing a catalog so another machine can query it are two different engineering problems, and Era 07 only solves the first one. Here's the plain version. A conversational layer reads relevant pieces of your catalog and phrases a natural answer for the person in front of it. That's flexible, and it's fast. But phrasing a good answer for a human is not the same thing as publishing a structured feed or endpoint that another piece of software can query deterministically, without a conversation happening in between. Most teams that get this right end up combining both. Structured fields carry the facts that need to be exact: price, stock position, part number. Retrieval handles the phrasing and context around those facts. That's the practical middle path, and you don't need a developer's vocabulary to manage it, just the discipline to keep both pieces current. If you want the retrieval mechanics underneath this, AI product search mechanics covers the deeper technical version. This section stays at the level an ops leader needs to make a decision, not the level a developer needs to build one. Here's the stake for the next era. Era 08 requires that same catalog to be queryable by another agent directly, with no human-phrased conversation standing between the question and the answer. Independent research backs up how early that stage still is: commercetools' AI-readiness research puts fewer than 5% of B2B organizations at the maturity stage that includes agent-to-agent transactions. Almost everyone reading this is somewhere behind that line, and that includes sellers who feel finished. What closes the gap between Era 07 and Era 08? Three things: structured price-tier exposure, consistent part-number and attribute tagging, and a feed or endpoint beyond the chat widget that another system can hit directly. None of those three is exotic. What's rare is having all three done well at once, and the evidence for that is uncomfortable. ChatSKU ran its own catalog agent-readability audit against 20 real B2B catalogs and found only 5 of the 20 served a product page an automated reader could actually use. Even sellers who assume they're ready mostly aren't, at the level sitting below the chat window. If the gap in your operation is upstream, in the export file itself rather than the website, the ERP export self-check is the field-level version of this test: part numbers, units of measure, tier pricing, all checked at the source before they ever reach a catalog assistant. One more term worth knowing exists, without needing to master it here: a structured feed built for machine querying increasingly follows one of a small set of emerging commerce protocols. The agentic commerce glossary is where those get defined properly. This piece isn't the place for that detail. On the practical side, ChatSKU ingests catalog data from PDF, Excel, and ERP exports without requiring a rebuild first. The catalog integration options page lists exactly what formats connect and how. What actually changes for your ops and sales team at Era 07? Reps stop fielding the same spec-and-price questions after hours, and quotes move from "wait for tomorrow" to "forwarded tonight." That's the practical shift, and it shows up in your team's calendar before it shows up in any dashboard. There's no B2B-specific study measuring exactly how much deflection or conversion lift comes from moving a catalog assistant from Era 06 to Era 07 specifically. Say that plainly instead of borrowing a number from a different industry or inventing one that sounds right. What does exist is evidence that buyers notice and act on the difference between a good and bad buying experience. Sana Commerce's 2025 buyer report found 75% of B2B buyers would switch suppliers for a better online buying experience. That's not a deflection rate for your specific setup, but it's a clear signal that the gap this article describes is one buyers actually feel and act on. Once the structural pieces from the previous section are in place, it's worth running your catalog back through the nine eras breakdown to confirm the score moved. A secondary check worth bookmarking alongside it: score your catalog maturity against a broader set of readiness criteria, not just the five measures this piece has walked through. People also ask Is a chat widget the same as being AI-ready? No. A chat widget can answer questions instantly and still fail the readiness test if it's trained on policies rather than your catalog. Run the self-test in this article on your own widget: ask it a real spec-and-price question and see whether it answers or hands off. How do I know what era my catalog is actually in? Score it yourself against the five measures in the 9 Eras tool rather than guessing from how modern your website looks. The tool is self-diagnostic, not a benchmark against other companies, so your result reflects your own setup. What's the difference between Era 07 and Era 08? Era 07 answers a human in natural language, in seconds, from the catalog itself. Era 08 requires that same catalog to be queryable directly by another piece of software, with no human-phrased conversation in between. Conclusion Your chat widget answers people. That's Era 07, and it's real progress, not a consolation prize. Era 08 requires answering software directly, and that's a different, harder claim. Era 07 is the necessary step between where most sellers are and where the market is heading. It just isn't the finish line the widget's sales pitch implied. The fastest way to find out where your own catalog actually sits is to run the self-test from this article this week, on a real question, with a real SKU. See the live demo Frequently asked questions What does "AI-enabled ChatCommerce" mean? It's the era where a catalog answers a buyer's question in its own words, down to the spec, with tier-aware pricing surfaced as part of the conversation. It's defined by the catalog doing the answering, not by having any chat interface at all. Why isn't Era 07 fully machine-readable? Because a conversational layer is built to phrase a good answer for a human, not to expose data in a format another system can query on its own. Those are separate engineering problems, and Era 07 only solves the first. Do I need to rebuild my website to reach Era 07? No. Catalog assistants like ChatSKU connect to existing PDF, Excel, and ERP data with a single line of code, without replatforming or migrating your product data first. What comes after Era 07? Era 08, Agentic Commerce, where the buyer on the other end is often software rather than a person, and that software needs to query your catalog directly rather than have a conversation with it. How long does it take to move from Era 06 to Era 07? Hours to days for the technical deployment itself, since it connects to catalog files you already have. The honest caveat: how long it takes to get your price-tier and spec data clean enough to answer well depends entirely on how organized that data already is.

2869.title: We tested 20 real B2B catalogs to see what AI agents can actually read
2869.text: Executive summary On 8 September 2026 we pointed an automated reader at 20 real B2B catalogs. Only 5 of them served a product page it could read. We expected to find gatekeeping. We found the opposite. Of the 13 robots.txt files we could read, zero blocked any of the 12 AI agents we checked. Nobody was shutting the door on purpose. The refusals happened somewhere else entirely. Seven of the 20 would not answer an automated request at all. Of the 13 that did answer, 7 exposed no product URL a machine could find, and 1 returned an error on the product page itself. So the published policy says come in. The plumbing says no. That is a very different problem, and a much more fixable one. Introduction Fifteen of twenty B2B catalogs gave an automated reader nothing usable at product level. That is the finding. We ran it ourselves, today, and you can re-run it. No survey. No vendor report. Two scripts, 20 named distributors and manufacturers, one product page each. Here is why we bothered. Buyers are increasingly sending software ahead of themselves, which is what agentic commerce means in practice. That software reads whatever your site hands it and scores you on that alone. It does not call to clarify. It does not fill in your form. If it cannot find your part number, your price, or your stock position, you are simply not on the short list. We assumed the industry was quietly locking AI crawlers out while legal figured out a position. The doors were unlocked. There was just nothing behind most of them a machine could read. What did we test, and how? Twenty public B2B catalogs, one product page each, on 8 September 2026. Every number in this post comes from that run. Here is the full list, so you can check our work: Grainger, McMaster-Carr, Fastenal, MSC Industrial, Motion Industries, Applied Industrial, Zoro, Global Industrial, DigiKey, Mouser, Newark, Allied Electronics, Ferguson, Wesco, Border States, Rexel USA, Hisco, Kaman, Genuine Parts, and Sonepar. All are real distributors or manufacturers. None is a competitor of ours. The method was deliberately boring: One request per host. We asked for robots.txt, then for a single product page. No crawling, no load. The site chose the product page. We took it from the company's own declared sitemap, or failing that from a product link on its own homepage. We used a normal desktop browser User-Agent. This is the friendly version of the test. A crawler identifying honestly as GPTBot or ClaudeBot would very likely do worse, not better. JavaScript was not executed. Some AI crawlers render pages. Others do not. What we measured is what a non-rendering retrieval client receives. n = 20, one page each. This is an audit, not a statistical sample. We report counts, never percentages of the industry. The scripts are re-runnable and the results are a snapshot dated 8 September 2026. Sites change. Ours might have changed by the time you read this, and so might theirs. Is anyone blocking AI agents on purpose? No. Not one of them. Robots.txt is the plain text file at the root of a website that tells automated readers which parts they may fetch. It is the closest thing the web has to a published door policy. Of the 13 catalogs whose robots.txt we could read, zero blocked any of the 12 AI agents we tested . That list included GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, ChatGPT-User, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, Google-Extended, CCBot, Amazonbot, and Bytespider. Not a single Disallow rule aimed at any of them. Whatever your board thinks the industry position is on AI crawlers, the published position is open. The other 7 robots.txt files could not be read at all. Which is a finding of its own. Then why did 7 of 20 refuse the connection? Bot protection at the edge, almost certainly. Not policy. Seven hosts would not answer a plain automated request at all. This happened before any question of content, markup, or product data. The connection itself was the problem. What happened Count What it means HTTP 403, refused 5 of 20 Something in front of the site decided the request was not a person Connection timed out 2 of 20 No answer at all within the wait window Answered the connection 13 of 20 Got as far as the content question Remember the User-Agent detail. We were presenting as an ordinary desktop browser and still got shut out. An agent that identified itself honestly would have a harder time, not an easier one. This is the gap that should worry you most, because it is invisible from the inside. The policy layer says yes. The edge layer says no. The person who wrote your robots.txt is rarely the person who configured your bot protection, and neither one is checking the other's work. How many catalogs gave an agent a product page it could read? Five of twenty. Work through the 13 that answered. Seven exposed no product URL at all that could be found in their sitemap or in their homepage HTML. A sitemap is the machine-readable index of a site's pages, and if products are missing from it, an agent has no path in. In most of those cases the category menus and product links are built by JavaScript after the page loads. A person sees a full catalog. A non-rendering client sees a shell with no way through to a product. One more returned an error on the product page itself , after serving robots.txt without complaint. So the door opened, then the room was locked. That leaves 5 of 20 catalogs that put a readable product page in front of an automated reader. If you want the mechanics of what happens next, we have written up how AI product search works once the data is actually reachable. What was on the five pages that did answer? Less than you would guess. And the gaps were not deliberate. Structured data is a labelled copy of the facts on a page, written for machines, so software does not have to guess which number on screen is the price. Schema.org is the shared vocabulary most search engines and AI systems use for those labels. Catalog Visible words Structured data Price in structured data Availability Kaman 1,721 Yes, not Product schema No No Global Industrial 784 Yes, not Product schema Yes Yes Zoro 689 Yes, full Product schema Yes Yes Unnamed catalog 1 115 None No No Unnamed catalog 2 75 None No No Two of the five are unnamed on purpose. Their pages are built by JavaScript, so an agent that renders may well see a full product page where our non-rendering client saw a stub. Naming them would be a claim our method cannot support. Across all five: schema.org Product markup on 1 of 5 . Price in structured data on 2 of 5 . Availability on 2 of 5 . A manufacturer part number or GTIN in structured data on 2 of 5 . The bright spots deserve names. Zoro was the only site of the twenty with full Product structured data. Global Industrial published price and availability in structured data and backed it with an 18-row spec table. Kaman served the deepest readable page in the set at 1,721 words, with a 25-row spec table. Now the detail that reframes everything. Zero of the five put a login or a quote wall in the way. Nothing was being withheld as strategy. The data simply was not in the HTML. And two of the five returned under 200 visible words. A buyer sees a full page. A retrieval client sees a headline and a menu. What this audit does not prove Plenty. We would rather say it than have you find it. Twenty hosts and one product page each is an audit, not a survey of the industry. Treat every number here as "5 of 20", never as a percentage of B2B distribution. We also cannot tell you what any of this costs anyone. No revenue figure, no conversion figure, and no lost-deal estimate can be honestly derived from a set of 20 page fetches. Anyone selling you one from data like this is guessing. And JavaScript rendering is a real variable, not a technicality. Some agents render. Some do not. A catalog that fails our test may pass for a different reader tomorrow. What should you check on your own catalog this week? Six things. None of them needs a project, and most take under an hour. Read your own product page with JavaScript disabled. Or just view the page source. If the price, specs, and stock line are not in the text, an agent may never see them. Ask whoever runs your bot protection what it does to non-browser traffic. Your robots.txt can say yes while your edge quietly says no. Nobody finds this out by accident. Open your sitemap and search it for a product URL. If products are not listed, an agent has no route to them. Confirm price and availability exist as labelled data , not only as styled text inside a widget that loads late. Check that part numbers and cross-references are on the page as text. A buyer holding a rival's number should still land on yours. Count how much sits behind a login. Not one of our five readable pages used a wall, so the assumption that everybody gates this data is worth re-testing. If the failure is in your source data rather than your site, start upstream. Our ERP export self-check covers the file itself: field integrity, duplicate SKUs, units of measure, price tiers. This post covers the website. They are two different surfaces and both can fail independently. For the wider business case, we have argued elsewhere why machine-readable catalogs are becoming a commercial requirement rather than an IT preference. Now the part we should say plainly, because we sell something in this market. ChatSKU does not fix what this audit measured. Adding an assistant to a page does not make that page readable to a crawler that never runs your JavaScript. If your product page returns 75 words to a machine today, it returns 75 words tomorrow with a widget on it. The six checks above are the fix for that, and most of them belong to whoever owns your front end and your bot protection. Server-rendered facts, labelled price and availability, a sitemap that lists products, and an edge policy that matches your robots.txt. What we do is the next moment, not that one. Once a buyer or an assistant is on your site, ChatSKU answers product questions from the catalog files your team already maintains, without a replatform. The two problems are worth separating: one decides whether you make the short list, the other decides what happens when someone arrives. If you are weighing them, our B2B catalog chatbot guide and the ROI calculator are the places to start. Because it was built for distributors and wholesalers , buyer-specific pricing tiers are native rather than bolted on, and the full list of ChatSKU's catalog integrations is here. People also ask Does blocking AI crawlers protect my catalog data? It might protect it from being copied. It will not protect your position on a short list. In our run, blocking was not the reason 15 of 20 catalogs came back empty. Broken access and missing labels were. Is a 403 error to an AI agent a security setting or a mistake? Usually neither, exactly. It is bot protection doing the job it was configured to do, before anyone considered that some bots are now buyers. It is a settings conversation, not a rebuild. If my site works fine for Google, will it work for AI agents? Not necessarily. Google has rendered JavaScript for years and has a crawl budget you cannot buy. A retrieval client fetching one page in real time has neither. How many products need to be readable before this matters? Start with the ones you actually want to sell. Your top movers, your stocked lines, and anything with a cross-reference. Fixing 200 pages that earn revenue beats fixing 40,000 that do not. Conclusion Twenty catalogs. Not one blocking AI agents by published policy. Five with a product page a machine could read. The gap is not permission. It is plumbing and labels, and both of those are yours to fix. So run the test yourself this week. Open your best-selling product page with JavaScript disabled, and read what is left on the screen. That is your catalog as software sees it. If what is left is a headline and a menu, you already know what to do first. See the live demo Frequently asked questions What exactly did you test on each of the 20 catalogs? Two things. Whether robots.txt allowed 12 named AI agents, and what a single product page returned to a non-rendering client. One request per host, on 8 September 2026. Why report counts instead of percentages? Because 20 hosts is not a sample of an industry. "5 of 20" is a fact about 20 catalogs. "25% of B2B distributors" would be a claim we cannot support, and you should distrust anyone who makes it from a set this size. Would the results change if the test executed JavaScript? For some sites, yes. Two of the five readable pages would very likely look much fuller. The 7 refused connections and the 7 with no findable product URL would not improve, because those failed before rendering was ever a question. What is structured data, in one sentence? It is a labelled copy of the facts already on your page, written in a format software can read without guessing which number is the price and which is the part number. Do I need structured data if I already have a catalog assistant on my site? They cover different moments. An assistant answers a buyer who has arrived. Structured data helps software decide whether to arrive at all. Most catalogs benefit from both, and the second one is cheaper than it sounds. Can I re-run this audit on my own catalog? Yes, and you should. Fetch your robots.txt in a browser, then view the page source on a product page and search it for your price and stock text. That is the entire test in five minutes.

2831.title: What is agentic commerce? A plain-English guide for B2B owners
2831.text: Executive summary Agentic commerce means the thing reading your website is increasingly software, not a person. And software that cannot find your answer does not call you back. It leaves you off the list. The buying has not been automated. The choosing has. Your customer still signs the order, but the short list gets drawn before anyone at your company hears from anybody. This guide answers the four questions owners actually ask. Does it replace your sales reps. Are your customers already doing it. What happens to your margin. And do you need a developer to deal with any of it. Introduction It is two o'clock on an ordinary Tuesday. Something arrives at your website looking for a half-inch stainless fitting in a pressure rating you stock. It reads three pages. It cannot work out whether the part ships this week. So it leaves. Nobody at your company ever knows it happened. No call, no email, no form, no abandoned cart. Your inside sales desk had a quiet afternoon, and a competitor picked up a line on a quote. That is the part people miss. This is not an after-hours story. It happens in daylight with your whole team at their desks. Here is the plain version. The buyer sent an assistant instead of calling, and the assistant will not ask a follow-up question. A person who cannot find the answer picks up the phone. Software that cannot find the answer scores you lower and moves on. No acronyms in this piece. No platform project. No assumption that you employ anybody who writes code. What is agentic commerce, in plain language? Agentic commerce is when the thing asking about your products is software, not a person. It decides on its own. Nobody rings your office. It compares, it ranks, it builds a short list. It finishes before anyone at your company hears from a human being. Now the part that should make you feel less like a beginner. You have been selling to software since 1979. Electronic purchase orders replaced phoned and faxed orders decades ago. If your company is over a certain size, you already have customers whose systems send orders with nobody typing them. You built that. It works. Agentic commerce is the same idea, minus the eighteen-month onboarding project and minus the agreement signed in advance. The old way: you and your customer agreed on a format and connected the pipes. Everybody knew it was coming. The new way: the buyer's software shows up at your website and reads whatever it can find. No agreement. No warning. That is the whole difference. It is also why this feels new when the underlying idea is forty-seven years old. If someone technical on your team wants the vocabulary, our agentic commerce glossary covers the terms. Does this replace your sales reps? No, and the data leans the other way. Gartner published a survey in May 2026. In it, 69% of B2B buyers said they check what AI told them with a sales rep. The software gathers. The human confirms. Gartner also predicts that by 2030, 75% of B2B buyers will prefer sales experiences that put human interaction first. Sit with that, because it is odd. The same firm forecasting that most B2B buying will run through AI is also forecasting buyers swinging back toward people. Nobody knows which wins. Anyone who says they do is selling something. What is not in dispute is which work the software takes first. It takes the part of your rep's day that was never selling anyway. The stock check. The price confirmation. The spec lookup your best rep has answered ten times this week and will answer ten more next week. That is not a relationship. It is a lookup. Your rep becomes the person the buyer calls to check the software's answer. That is a role change, not a redundancy. There is a quieter benefit in there too. Reps buried in lookups are why quotes take two days, which is the response gap faster competitors keep beating you on. Are your customers actually doing this yet? More than you think. And more than you think they think. Deloitte's B2B agentic research found that 40% of B2B buyers already use agentic AI in purchasing, against 24% of suppliers. Your customers moved first. They usually do. Deloitte also found that 72% of suppliers describe their sales process as mostly or highly automated. Only 47% of buyers agree. Read those two numbers slowly. Seven in ten suppliers believe they have this handled. Fewer than five in ten of their customers agree. That gap is not about technology. It is about self-perception, and it is the most uncomfortable finding in the pile. Then there is timing. Forrester's 2026 predictions put one in five B2B sellers into agent-led quote negotiation during this year. So much for waiting until 2030. Now the honest part, and it matters more than any number above. Nobody has measured this in industrial distribution specifically. The published research covers software buyers, enterprise procurement teams, and retail. There is no study of what a fastener distributor's customers are doing on a Tuesday, and we will not pretend otherwise. What the research does establish is direction. Everywhere it has been measured, buyers are ahead of sellers. If software only sees your price, what happens to your margin? You lose on price, because price is the only thing you gave it to compare. Think about a load board. A carrier does not win a load because the dispatcher likes them. They win it because their rate, their lane, and their availability were legible on a screen when the load posted. Nobody there gets credit for being good on the phone. Agentic commerce is a load board being built around your product catalog. And most catalogs today publish exactly one comparable fact. There is a sharper version of the risk. When the buyer's software and the seller's software negotiate, both walk straight down toward the seller's floor price. Neither has a reason to stop. There is no relationship in the room to slow it down. So the counter is not secrecy. The counter is giving the software more to look at than a number. Availability. Lead time. Contract terms. Whether you can actually fill the order Thursday. Whether your cross-references are accurate, so a buyer holding a rival's part number still lands on yours. Those facts win business every day on the phone. They are just not written down anywhere software can reach. If the only easy-to-find fact about your company is a price, that price is your entire pitch. That is the real business case for an AI-ready product catalog . We are not going to invent a dollar figure for what ignoring this costs you, because nobody has a credible one. If you want a number, model your own numbers against your quote volume. Do you need to hire a developer to deal with this? Not to start. The first moves are business decisions, not engineering ones. Decide what you are actually willing to publish. Most suppliers hide price out of habit rather than strategy. Some of that habit protects real margin. Some of it quietly costs you inclusion. Separating the two is your call, not a developer's. Get stock and lead time somewhere a stranger can reach. If your own website cannot say whether a part ships this week, nothing else on this list matters yet. Make your product information say what your reps say. If your best rep knows five things about a part that appear nowhere in your catalog, your catalog is not describing your business. Stop hiding the facts a buyer needs to choose you. Every one of them is something you already give away freely, one phone call at a time. If someone at your company runs the systems, give them one job. Our ERP export self-check runs about ten minutes and names the product fields you are missing. This is where ChatSKU fits, and we will be specific about it. It reads the catalog files you already have. A PDF price list, a spreadsheet, an ERP extract. Then it answers buyer questions from them. One line of code on your site. No rebuild, no migration. It was built for manufacturers and distributors , which is why customer groups and tiered pricing sit inside it rather than bolted on. Here is what ChatSKU connects to . People also ask Is agentic commerce the same as a chat window on a website? No. A chat window waits to be asked. Agentic software goes looking, compares, and decides on its own. For the category explainer, start with what a B2B catalog chatbot actually does. Which orders will software buy first? The routine third of your order book. Commodity items, small repeat spend, straight reorders. Not the eleven-year account with redlined terms behind it. Complexity is a slow lane for software, and most of your best business lives there. Can a small distributor compete when software is choosing? Yes, and being small may be the opening. Software carries no incumbent bias. It does not know who has more branches or four decades in the trade. It knows only what it can read. Is anyone in industrial distribution actually doing this yet? Not in a confirmed, published way. Amazon Business has shipped buyer-facing AI tools, so the direction is not theoretical. But nobody in this trade has a verified agentic purchasing setup you can go and look at. Early is not behind. Conclusion Agentic commerce is not robots buying things from you. It is software deciding whether you are worth asking, using only what it can find. The buying has not been automated. The choosing has. That is the entire story, and it is happening at two in the afternoon on ordinary Tuesdays. So here is one thing to do this week. Open your own website as a stranger and ask it three questions. What does this cost, do you have it, and when does it ship. If you cannot get all three answers without a phone call, neither can your buyer's software. See the live demo Frequently asked questions What does agentic commerce mean in one sentence? It means software, not a person, researching and short-listing suppliers for a buyer. The short list then goes to the human who signs. Will an AI agent negotiate my prices down? It will try, and it has no built-in reason to stop. Your protection is not secrecy. It is giving the software facts other than price to weigh, starting with availability and lead time. Do I have to publish my pricing publicly to be included? No, but you do have to publish something. And think about what you already accept. Every time you pull a credit report, you let software judge a customer's finances. You never re-verify that score yourself. The unfamiliar part is not software deciding. It is software deciding about you. What if the software gets my product specs wrong? It happens, and it lands on your reputation either way. An assistant answering from thin information will fill the gaps itself. That makes it a data problem before it is an AI problem. What is the first thing I should do about this in the next ninety days? Find out what your own website tells a stranger about stock, lead time, and price. Write down every question it cannot answer. That list is your project plan, and no developer is needed to write it.

2783.title: Response gap by industry: hardware vs electronics vs industrial supply
2783.text: Executive summary The response gap is not one number. Hardware, electronics, and industrial supply all lose deals to slow replies, but they lose them to three different clocks. See how this plays out for DFW distributors, manufacturers and wholesalers . In hardware the clock is breadth. In electronics it is availability. In industrial supply it is downtime. The same four-hour delay is survivable in one, expensive in the second, and account-ending in the third. That matters because most distributors measure a single average response time across the whole business. An average hides the segment where the delay actually costs you money. Introduction Ask three distributors what a slow quote costs them and you will get three different answers. The fastener supplier talks about volume. The component distributor talks about allocation. The MRO supplier talks about a plant manager who stopped calling. They are all describing the response gap , which is how long a buyer waits between asking you something and getting a real answer. They are not describing the same problem. This post breaks the gap down by segment. What the buyer is actually waiting for, what the delay costs, and which number you should be watching. One thing to be straight about first. There is no credible published benchmark that measures response times separately for these three industries. What follows is a structural argument built on how each business actually works, not a table of survey figures we cannot source. Why does the response gap look different in every industry? Because the buyer is not waiting for the same thing. A response gap is only expensive when the delay changes the outcome. What changes the outcome differs by what you sell. In one segment the buyer simply moves on. In another your answer goes stale while it sits in a queue. In a third the buyer is losing money every hour they wait. So the useful question is not "how fast do we reply." It is "what is the buyer's deadline, and are we inside it." Those are different questions and they produce different priorities. Hardware and fasteners: the breadth clock In hardware the response gap is a volume problem hiding inside a workload problem. Catalogs here run to tens of thousands of near-identical line items. Bolts, anchors, fittings, and brackets that differ by a thread pitch, a coating, or a grade. Unit values are low and requests usually arrive as lists rather than single items. That combination produces a quiet failure. Quoting a forty-line list by hand takes real time, and the order it produces may be worth a few hundred dollars. A rep with a full inbox will work the large opportunity first. That is a rational choice and it is also why the requests easiest to win are the ones that sit longest. The cost never appears as a lost deal you can name. It appears as volume that quietly went somewhere else, because the buyer needed availability and price on a list and took the first supplier who confirmed both. The number to watch here is not average response time. It is the share of multi-line requests that get a complete answer on the first reply. Partial answers restart the clock. Electronics components: the availability clock In electronics the delay does not just annoy the buyer. It can make your answer wrong. Component buyers are asking availability questions, and availability moves. According to ECIA's breakdown of semiconductor lead times , complex wafer fabrication alone takes up to 12 weeks, assembly and test add another 4 to 8, and the full cycle runs roughly 26 weeks. Distributors in that channel hold around 180 days of inventory. Your buyer cannot influence any of it. They are working inside a cycle measured in months and trying to land parts against a build date. ECIA also notes what happens when supply tightens: customers double order. That behaviour ripples through the channel as a bullwhip, and it means a position you quoted on Monday may not be the position you can honour on Thursday. So the response gap here has a second cost on top of the lost sale. A slow reply produces a stale reply. The buyer who waits three days for a stock position, then finds it gone at the PO stage, learns something about you that a fast "no, but here is the alternate" would never have taught them. The number to watch is the age of your answer at the moment the buyer reads it, not the time it took to write. Industrial supply and MRO: the downtime clock In industrial supply the buyer is not shopping. Something is broken. An emergency MRO request is a symptom of a stopped line, and the economics of a stopped line are brutal. Senseye and Siemens put the scale of it plainly in The True Cost of Downtime 2024 . The world's 500 largest companies lose almost $1.4 trillion a year to unplanned downtime, equal to 11% of their revenues. Per hour, the numbers vary enormously by sector. An hour in a large automotive plant costs $2.3 million, more than $600 a second. At the other end, an hour in fast moving consumer goods costs about $36,000. The average large plant still loses 27 hours a month. Read those figures carefully. They describe what your customer loses while their line is stopped, not how long distributors take to reply. That is exactly the point. The buyer's cost of waiting is orders of magnitude larger than the value of the order they are placing with you. Which is why the response gap in MRO does not cost you a quote. It costs you the account. A buyer who could not reach you during a stoppage will make sure they never depend on you during the next one. The number to watch is time to a usable answer during the buyer's emergency, not your average across all inquiries. How the three compare Same gap, three different mechanisms. Segment What the buyer is waiting for What a slow reply costs The metric that matters Hardware and fasteners Price and availability across a long list Volume, quietly, with no named lost deal Share of multi-line requests answered completely on the first reply Electronics components Stock position, alternates, and lead time The sale, plus credibility when the answer goes stale Age of the answer when the buyer reads it Industrial supply and MRO Can you get this part to me today The account, not just the order Time to a usable answer during a stoppage Notice that none of the three is solved by simply telling the team to reply faster. They need different things answered, at different speeds, with different tolerances for being wrong. Are you measuring the wrong clock? Most distributors track one average response time for the whole business. That single number is close to useless once you have more than one type of buyer. An average blends a same-day MRO emergency with a routine fastener list and a component availability check. Improve the easy segment and the average moves. The segment that was actually costing you money stays exactly where it was. Three questions worth asking at your next pipeline review: Which segment has the widest spread? Not the worst average, the widest range between your fastest and slowest reply. Spread is where the losses hide. What percentage of first replies are complete answers? A holding message that promises a quote tomorrow has not closed the gap, it has documented it. What happens to inquiries that arrive after hours? A machine that fails at 6pm does not wait for your morning. Neither does the buyer. If you want to put a number on what the delay is worth in your own business, our ROI calculator works from your own inquiry volume rather than a benchmark from someone else's company. What actually closes the gap in each segment The fix is the same shape in all three, but the priority order changes. In hardware, the win is completeness at speed on long lists. That is a data problem before it is a staffing problem. If your catalog can be queried directly, a forty-line list stops being a forty-line task. In electronics, the win is freshness. An answer that reflects the current position beats a more detailed answer written yesterday, and offering a named alternate immediately beats a perfect reply that arrives after the buyer has committed elsewhere. In MRO, the win is availability at the moment of the emergency, which usually means outside business hours. That is the clearest case for something that answers when nobody is at a desk. All three point at the same underlying constraint, which is that answers currently require a person. We covered that dependency in the human bottleneck , and the practical sequence for getting first replies under an hour is laid out in three steps to quote in under an hour . An AI catalog assistant closes the gap by answering the first question directly from your existing catalog data, at any hour, and handing a qualified request to your team with the details already gathered. It does not replace the rep on the complex quote. It removes the delay before the rep ever sees it. You can see what it connects to on the features page , and how it fits distributors, manufacturers, and wholesalers specifically. People also ask Which industry has the worst response gap? There is no published benchmark that measures response times separately by industry, so any ranking you see is an estimate rather than a measurement. The more useful comparison is cost of delay. In MRO the buyer's hourly losses dwarf the order value, which makes the same delay far more damaging than it would be on a routine fastener list. Is the response gap just a staffing problem? Usually not. Adding headcount raises capacity during business hours but does nothing for inquiries that arrive at night or on weekends. It also does not make a forty-line list faster to quote. The full definition of the response gap treats it as a timing problem for exactly that reason. What counts as fast enough on a B2B quote? It depends which clock the buyer is on. An emergency MRO request needs an answer in minutes to be useful. A routine component availability check needs an answer while the position is still accurate. A multi-line hardware list needs a complete answer before a competitor sends one. Should we set different response targets for different product lines? Yes, and most distributors do not. A single service level across a mixed catalog will be too slow for emergencies and unnecessarily strict for routine orders. Segment the target by what the buyer is waiting for. Conclusion Hardware, electronics, and industrial supply do not share a response gap. They share a symptom. Work out which clock your buyers are on, then measure against that instead of a single company-wide average. The segment with the widest spread between your fastest and slowest reply is almost always where the money is going. See the live demo Frequently asked questions What is the response gap? It is how long a buyer waits between raising an inquiry and receiving a real answer. Not an acknowledgement, an answer. We define it in full in what is the response gap , and the response gap page shows what closing it looks like in practice. Why can't we just measure average response time? An average across a mixed catalog blends emergencies with routine orders. Improving the easy segment moves the average while the expensive segment stays broken. Track the spread and segment the measurement. Does this apply to distributors with only a few thousand SKUs? Yes. How deep your variants run matters far more than how many items you list. A few thousand parts separated by grade, thread, or tolerance create the same quoting workload as a much larger catalog of plainly distinct products. How does after-hours inquiry volume change the picture? It changes it most in MRO, where failures do not follow business hours, and least in routine hardware ordering. If you have never measured what share of your inquiries arrive outside working hours, that number usually surprises people. Do faster replies hurt quote quality? They do if speed means guessing. They do not if the first answer comes straight from your catalog data rather than from someone's memory. The risk is not speed, it is answering from the wrong source. Where do RFQ workflows fit into this? An RFQ form is where a qualified request gets captured, but the gap opens before that, while the buyer is still deciding whether you are worth asking. Our guide to RFQ automation for manufacturers covers the workflow side. What should we fix first? Whichever segment has the widest spread between your fastest and slowest reply. That is where a fix produces the largest change, and it is usually not the segment your team complains about most.

2684.title: Is your ERP export AI-agent-friendly? A 10-minute self-check
2684.text: Executive Summary Your ERP already "exports" your product data. That's not the same thing as an export an AI agent can read correctly. Most of these files were built for a different job: feeding a warehouse system, populating a price list, syncing item numbers into another piece of software. Nobody asked whether the file could also answer a buyer's spec question without guessing. Ten specific, checkable properties determine whether it can. Not a philosophy about "clean data." Ten things you can open a file and look at right now. This is a technical audit, not a vendor pitch. You can run every checkpoint below against your own export in the next ten minutes, and you don't need to buy anything to do it. The ten checkpoints, grouped into four stages: Do you know your export's native format? Does a GTIN or long numeric ID survive the export intact? Does the field selection include what buyers actually ask about? Are there duplicate SKUs in the file? Do your data sources agree with each other? Does every product carry a classification code? Does that classification carry actual attributes, or just a bucket? Is unit of measure explicit and consistent? Do you know if the file is a snapshot or a live signal? Does pricing reflect customer groups, or one flat price? Introduction Someone just asked whether your catalog is ready for an AI assistant to read. A vendor, a sales director, maybe your own curiosity. You said "we already have an export," pulled it up, and realized you don't actually know if that's true. "We have an export" and "our export is AI-agent-ready" are different claims. An export that has run fine for years, feeding your warehouse system or a legacy price list, can still fail every one of the checkpoints below, because it was never built to answer a buyer's question on its own. If you want the fuller vocabulary behind terms like GTIN, UNSPSC, and EDI before you start, the agentic commerce glossary covers those definitions. If you want the business case rather than the audit, that argument lives in AI-ready catalogs for autonomous buying . This piece assumes you already know roughly what these terms are and puts them to work as a checklist instead. What kind of export file do you actually have? Before you check data quality, you need to know exactly what format and mechanism produced the file sitting in front of you. Most of the checkpoints below only make sense once you've answered this one. Do you know your export's native format? Test: name the exact format your product data leaves your ERP in, out loud, right now. Not "a spreadsheet" or "an export." A flat CSV or Excel pull? A structured feed like SAP's IDoc/MATMAS06? A REST/OData API call with a defined query? If you run SAP, this matters more than it looks like it should. SAP's native way of distributing material master data is the IDoc, specifically the MATMAS06 message type, a segment-based, EDI-like format, not a flat file. Some S/4HANA shops instead use the newer "Export Master Data" app for flat-file extracts, or pull fields directly via OData. Two SAP shops can hand you two structurally different things and both call it "the export." See SAP IDoc documentation if you want to confirm which one you're actually looking at. If your "ERP" is really a WooCommerce store with a B2B pricing plugin bolted on, the export mechanics are different again, and worth checking separately in the WooCommerce B2B data guide . Magento and Adobe Commerce shops face a similar translation step, covered in the Magento B2B integration guide . Pass: you can name the format specifically, and you know roughly when it was last touched. Fail: "someone set this up a while back" is the honest answer. What breaks: if nobody currently knows which fields survived translation from the source system, an assistant built against an outdated field mapping keeps answering with a value, a price, a spec, that was correct in the old format but got silently dropped or renamed after a later system upgrade. It doesn't know it's wrong. It just answers. Does a GTIN or long numeric ID survive the export intact? Test: open the file, find the GTIN, UPC, or EAN column, and check five random rows for the full digit string. Pass: the full 12 to 14 digit identifier is intact as text, including any leading zeros. Fail: it displays as scientific notation, something like 1.23457E+12, or the leading zeros are gone. This is the default behavior when a CSV with no type information gets opened in Excel, and it's a documented, verified NetSuite CSV export behavior. It's also the single easiest thing on this whole list to check yourself in under a minute. What breaks: an assistant matching a buyer's barcode scan or GTIN lookup against a mangled ID gets a value that matches nothing, or worse, matches the wrong product because two different GTINs rounded to the same corrupted number. GTIN is only useful as a stable identifier if it stays exact. GS1 governs the standard for exactly this reason; see the GS1 GTIN standard if you want the source. If your export comes from an API call, does the field selection include what buyers actually ask about? Test: pull up the field or query definition behind the export, the `$select` list, or whatever fields an integrator originally chose, and compare it against what your sales team actually fields most: price, stock quantity, category, lead time. If you run Dynamics 365 Business Central, this is worth double-checking specifically. Items are exposed through a documented REST/OData API where `$select` controls exactly which fields come back, and the older page-based OData v4 endpoints are being retired in favor of `/api/v2.0/`. Two Business Central shops can hand over structurally different exports depending on when their integration was built, and which fields someone selected at the time. For Epicor and Infor, the field structure varies enough by implementation that there isn't one clean answer here. Check your own integration's field list directly rather than assuming it matches a generic template. Pass: price, stock, category, and lead time are all explicitly selected fields, not assumed or missing. Fail: the integration was built for a narrower original purpose, syncing item numbers into a warehouse system, say, and buyer-relevant fields were never added. What breaks: the assistant has no price field to read. It either declines to answer, or if a similarly named stray field exists in the data, it quotes the wrong number with full confidence. Does your export have duplicate or conflicting records? Once you know your file's format, the next test is whether the records inside it are even internally trustworthy, before you worry about how rich or current they are. Are there duplicate SKUs in the file? Test: sort or pivot on the SKU or item-number column and look for repeats. Pass: every SKU appears exactly once. Fail: the same SKU shows up more than once. This usually happens when a legacy feed and a newer, manually maintained list both got merged into one export without anyone deduplicating them. What breaks: an assistant asked about that SKU now has two conflicting records to choose from. It either arbitrarily picks one, possibly the wrong one, or hedges with a vague "conflicting information" answer. Both look broken to a buyer who just wanted a straight answer. If your data comes from more than one source, do the sources agree? Test: pick five to ten SKUs that exist in both your primary ERP export and any secondary source (a manually maintained price sheet, an older catalog feed), then compare price and spec fields side by side. Pass: values match across sources for the same SKU. Fail: the ERP says one price, the manual sheet says another, and nobody has reconciled them recently. What breaks: the same buyer question, asked minutes apart, can return two different prices depending on which file happened to feed the assistant that day. That's the exact kind of inconsistency a human rep would never produce, and it's the fastest way to lose a buyer's trust in the assistant entirely. Can an AI agent actually filter and compare your products? Once your records are deduplicated and internally consistent, the next question is whether they're rich enough to support the comparative, spec-level questions buyers actually ask, not just a lookup by product name. Does every product carry a classification code? Test: check whether the category or classification column (a UNSPSC code, an ETIM class, or an internal category field) is populated on every row, not just some of them. Pass: populated on all or nearly all rows. Fail: blank on a meaningful share of rows, typically the older SKUs that predate whatever classification scheme you're currently using. What breaks: a buyer asking to see every enclosure rated for outdoor use gets no answer for the unclassified products, not because they're irrelevant, but because there's no category signal for the assistant to filter on. Those SKUs effectively disappear from comparison questions. Does your classification carry actual attributes, or just a bucket? This is worth stating plainly, because it's the checkpoint people skip past fastest. UNSPSC is a five-level procurement and spend classification code. By design, it carries no attribute payload. It tells you a product's category and nothing about its specs. ETIM and eCl@ss are different: they pair a category with a defined set of technical attributes and permitted values (voltage, IP rating, dimensions) per class. That difference is the whole ballgame for technical product lines. Test: check which standard your export actually uses, and whether attribute fields exist alongside the category code. Pass: for technical or spec-heavy lines (electrical, HVAC, industrial components), the export includes real attribute fields, not just a category code. Fail: a UNSPSC code and nothing else. The product is categorized, but it has no queryable specs attached. What breaks: the assistant can say "this is an enclosure," but it can't answer "what's the IP rating" or "is this compatible with a 24V system," because that data was never structured as its own field. UNSPSC alone was never built to answer that kind of question. Is unit of measure explicit and consistent? Test: check whether every priced line has a distinct UOM field (each, case, pallet, linear foot) and whether the price actually corresponds to that unit. Pass: UOM is its own field, and price always matches it. Fail: UOM is implied, inconsistent, or missing entirely. The same price column sometimes means "per each," sometimes "per case," with nothing flagging which is which. What breaks: the assistant quotes a number without the right unit, or with the wrong one, and a buyer assumes twelve dollars is per unit when it's actually per case of fifty. That's not a rounding error to a buyer. That's a quote they'll never trust again. Will your pricing and inventory data still be true tomorrow? The final stage isn't about the data's structure. It's about trust over time. Do you know what kind of signal you're actually holding, and does it reflect who's asking? Do you know whether this file is a catalog snapshot or a live inventory signal? Test: if your export is fed by or resembles an EDI transaction, check which transaction set it actually is. An 832 is a price and sales catalog. An 846 is an inventory inquiry or advice. An 850 is a purchase order, which pulls its item numbers and prices from the 832. Also check the file's own generation timestamp. Pass: you know which transaction type and timestamp you're handing over, and you know a catalog snapshot doesn't carry live stock levels by definition. Fail: an 832 catalog extract gets treated as a real-time inventory source, because it came from the ERP and that felt authoritative enough not to question further. What breaks: the assistant states or implies stock availability from a file that structurally has no inventory field in it. That's not what an 832 was built to carry. The buyer gets a stock claim backed by no actual data behind it. Does pricing reflect customer groups, or only one list price? Test: check whether the export includes a customer-group, contract-price, or tier field, or just a single flat price column regardless of buyer type. Pass: tier or group-specific pricing is present, and it's mapped to the right segment. Fail: one price per SKU, with no way to distinguish a list-price buyer from a contracted account. What breaks: the assistant quotes the same list price to every buyer, including the ones with negotiated contract terms. Tier-one pricing shown to a tier-three account, or the reverse. A pricing-integrity problem like this erodes trust the moment a contracted buyer notices the mismatch. If your export handles this well, that same tier data is worth connecting to your quote process; see RFQ automation for catalogs for how tiered pricing feeds into a quote workflow instead of just a lookup. What happens after your export passes this check? Run this check on the file before you send it anywhere, to ChatSKU or to any other tool that's going to answer buyer questions from it. A clean file makes setup faster and the answers more trustworthy, no matter which tool receives it. ChatSKU reads the file a customer actually sends: a PDF, an Excel sheet, an ERP export, or a CSV. Old, messy, scanned, or spread across multiple files. Our team configures the assistant against that file directly. We don't claim a live, automatic pull from SAP, NetSuite, or any other named ERP. If your export just passed most of the ten checkpoints above, that file is exactly what makes setup fast and the answers it produces trustworthy from day one. See what ChatSKU connects to for the full list of formats, or what a catalog assistant does if the category itself is new to you. The tool is built for manufacturers and distributors specifically, not retail catalogs retrofitted for B2B. People Also Ask What file format does my ERP actually export? It depends on your ERP and how the integration was originally built. SAP shops often have IDoc/MATMAS06 feeds rather than a flat file. NetSuite and most spreadsheet-era setups export CSV. Business Central exposes items through a REST/OData API with selectable fields. The honest answer for many readers is "I need to check," and checkpoint one above walks through how. Why does my GTIN show up as scientific notation in Excel? Because a plain CSV file carries no type information, so Excel guesses that a long digit string is a number and reformats it, often dropping leading zeros in the process. This is a documented NetSuite CSV export behavior, and it's not specific to that one platform. Opening the same column as text, rather than letting Excel auto-detect it, usually prevents it. What's the difference between UNSPSC and ETIM classification? UNSPSC is a procurement and spend classification code with no attribute payload by design. It tells you a product's category, not its specs. ETIM and eCl@ss pair a category with a defined set of technical attributes per class: voltage, dimensions, IP rating, and so on. If your products are technical or spec-heavy, UNSPSC alone won't support spec-level buyer questions. How often should I re-export my product data for an AI assistant? Often enough that price and stock fields stay accurate for whatever cadence your business actually changes them at: daily for fast-moving inventory, weekly or monthly for stable catalogs. The more useful question isn't frequency. It's whether you know if the file you're handing over is a snapshot or a live signal, which is checkpoint nine above. Conclusion Ten checkpoints, one file, ten minutes. That's the whole test. Most ERP exports weren't built with an AI agent in mind. That isn't a failure on your part. It just isn't what the original integration was built to do. If your file just failed a handful of these checks, you now know exactly which ones and why they matter mechanically, not just that "the data needs work." Fix the ones that broke first. A clean export makes any tool that reads it, ChatSKU included, faster to set up and more trustworthy to buyers from the first question they ask it. Talk to ChatSKU about your catalog Frequently Asked Questions What is the minimum file format an AI catalog assistant needs to work with? There's no single required format. A clean CSV or Excel export works, and so does a structured feed like an IDoc or an API pull, as long as the fields buyers actually ask about (price, stock, spec, unit of measure) are present and accurate. Format matters less than whether the ten checkpoints above pass. Can I use a plain CSV export, or do I need an API connection to my ERP? A plain CSV works fine, as long as it passes the checks above, particularly the GTIN scientific-notation check and the customer-group pricing check. An API connection isn't required to get started; it's a separate decision about how the file gets refreshed over time. What is GTIN scientific-notation corruption and how do I fix it? It's what happens when Excel opens a CSV with no type information and reformats a long numeric ID as a number instead of text, often losing digits or leading zeros in the process. Formatting the GTIN column as text before or during export, rather than letting Excel guess, prevents it. Is UNSPSC enough for AI-agent product matching, or do I need ETIM/eCl@ss?
